items.fingerprint: d4rt teaching ai to see the world in four dimensions|deepmind.google/blog/d4rt-teaching-ai-to-see-the-world-in-four-dimensions
items.title: D4RT: Teaching AI to see the world in four dimensions
items.description: D4RT: Unified, efficient 4D reconstruction and tracking up to 300x faster than prior methods.
items.content: January 22, 2026 Research D4RT: Teaching AI to see the world in four dimensions Guillaume Le Moing and Mehdi S. M. Sajjadi Introducing D4RT, a unified AI model for 4D scene reconstruction and tracking across space and time. Anytime we look at the world, we perform an extraordinary feat of memory and prediction. We see and understand things as they are at a given moment in time, as they were a moment ago, and how they are going to be in the moment to follow. Our mental model of the world maintains a persistent representation of reality and we use that model to draw intuitive conclusions about the causal relationship between the past, present and future. To help machines see the world more like we do, we can equip them with cameras, but that only solves the problem of input. To make sense of this input, computers must solve a complex, inverse problem: taking a video — which is a sequence of flat 2D projections — and recovering or understanding the rich, volumetric 3D world, in motion. Today, we are introducing D4RT (Dynamic 4D Reconstruction and Tracking) , a new AI model that unifies dynamic scene reconstruction into a single, efficient framework, bringing us closer to the next frontier of artificial intelligence: total perception of our dynamic reality. The Challenge of the Fourth Dimension In order for it to understand a dynamic scene captured on a 2D video, an AI model must track every pixel of every object as it moves through the three dimensions of space and the fourth dimension of time. In addition, it must disentangle this motion from the motion of the camera, maintaining a coherent representation even when objects move behind one another or leave the frame entirely. Traditionally, capturing this level of geometry and motion from 2D videos requires computationally intensive processes or a patchwork of specialized AI models — some for depth, others for movement or camera angles — resulting in AI reconstructions that are slow and fragmented. D4RT’s simplified architecture and novel query mechanism place it at the forefront of 4D reconstruction while being up to 300x more efficient than previous methods — fast enough for real-time applications in robotics, augmented reality, and more. How D4RT Works: A Query-Based Approach D4RT operates as a unified encoder-decoder Transformer architecture. The encoder first processes the input video into a compressed representation of the scene’s geometry and motion. Unlike older systems that employed separate modules for different tasks, D4RT calculates only what it needs using a flexible querying mechanism centered around a single, fundamental question: "Where is a given pixel from the video located in 3D space at an arbitrary time , as viewed from a chosen camera ?" Building on our prior work , a lightweight decoder then queries this representation to answer specific instances of the posed question. Because queries are independent, they can be processed in parallel on modern AI hardware. This makes D4RT extremely fast and scalable, whether it’s tracking just a few points or reconstructing an entire scene. Your browser does not support the video tag. D4RT combines a powerful encoder that builds a rich, global understanding of the video, and a lightweight decoder that answers thousands of queries in parallel. By asking specific questions — identifying where a source pixel is located at a target time and camera view — the model efficiently solves diverse tasks like tracking, depth estimation, and pose estimation through a single, flexible interface. Capabilities: Fast, Accurate 4D Understanding With this flexible formulation, a wide variety of 4D tasks can now be solved by the model, including: Point Tracking : By querying a pixel's location across different time steps, D4RT can predict its 3D trajectory. Importantly, an object need not be visible on other frames of the video for the model to make a prediction. Point Cloud Reconstruction : By freezing time and the camera viewpoint, D4RT can directly generate the complete 3D structure of a scene, eliminating extra steps such as separate camera estimation or per-video iterative optimization. Camera Pose Estimation : By generating and aligning 3D snapshots of a single moment from different viewpoints, D4RT can easily recover the camera's trajectory. As detailed in the underlying technical report , D4RT outperforms previous methods across a wide spectrum of 4D reconstruction tasks. Qualitative comparisons show that while other methods struggle with dynamic objects — often duplicating them or failing to reconstruct them entirely — D4RT maintains a solid, continuous understanding of the moving world. Crucially, D4RT’s precision does not come at the expense of efficiency. In testing, it performed 18x to 300x faster than the previous state of the art. For example, D4RT processed a one-minute video in roughly five seconds on a single TPU chip. Previous state-of-the-art methods could take up to ten minutes for the same task — an improvement of 120x. Slide 1 of 3 In evaluations on the MPI Sintel benchmark featuring complex synthetic scenes with fast motion blur and non-rigid deformation, D4RT demonstrates superior fidelity compared to recent strong baselines. This highlights the model’s ability to reconstruct geometry accurately even when objects or the camera move rapidly through the scene. Using smart-glasses footage from the Aria Digital Twin dataset, D4RT achieves top-tier performance in 3D point tracking. This verifies the model's robust handling of complex ego-motion and occlusions in realistic household environments. Evaluating camera pose estimation on the diverse indoor and outdoor scenes of the RE10k dataset, D4RT achieves the highest AUC score. This metric, which tracks how often the estimated pose falls within a range of strict accuracy thresholds, illustrates the model’s capacity to lock onto stable geometry without the need for costly test-time optimization. Downstream Applications D4RT demonstrates that we don't need to choose between accuracy and efficiency in 4D reconstruction. Its flexible, query-based system can capture our dynamic world in real-time, paving the way for the next generation of spatial computing. This includes: Robotics : Robots need to navigate dynamic environments populated by moving people and objects. D4RT can provide the spatial awareness required for safe navigation and dextrous manipulation. Augmented Reality (AR) : For AR glasses to overlay digital objects onto the real world, they need an instant, low-latency understanding of a scene’s geometry. D4RT’s efficiency contributes to making on-device deployment a tangible reality. World Models : By effectively disentangling camera motion, object motion, and static geometry, D4RT brings us a step closer to AI that possesses a true “world model” of physical reality — a necessary step on the path to AGI. We're continuing to explore the model’s capabilities and potential for applications across robotics, augmented reality, and beyond. items.title: Google DeepMind supports U.S. Department of Energy on Genesis: a national mission to accelerate innovation and scientific discovery
items.description: Google DeepMind and the DOE partner on Genesis, a new effort to accelerate science with AI.
items.content: December 18, 2025 Science Google DeepMind supports U.S. Department of Energy on Genesis: a national mission to accelerate innovation and scientific discovery Pushmeet Kohli and Tom Lue Your browser does not support the audio element. Listen to article 6 minutes We stand at an inflection point where the convergence of advanced AI and scientific research promises to unlock a new golden age of discovery . Recognizing this, we’re pleased to support the White House’s Genesis Mission - a historic national effort to use AI to transform how scientific research is conducted and accelerate the speed of American science. The Genesis Mission will mobilize the U.S. Department of Energy’s (DOE) 17 National Laboratories, industry and academia to build an integrated discovery platform, accelerating breakthroughs across the nation’s most pressing challenges including energy, scientific discovery, and national security. At Google DeepMind, our mission is to build AI responsibly to benefit humanity. There is perhaps no clearer expression of this than the application of AI within science. Scientists today face significant obstacles of unprecedented scale and complexity — from shaping and simulating the intricate dynamics of fusion plasma, to exploring the vast search space of new materials, and finding a way to process and understand ever-growing volumes of data and literature. Modern deep learning methods are uniquely suited to address these challenges and compress the time new discoveries would otherwise require. To help realize the ambitious vision in the Genesis Mission, Google and the DOE are partnering to support the Administration's goal of harnessing the AI and advanced computing revolution to dramatically expand the productivity and impact of American research and innovation within a decade. We see this as the beginning of an enduring partnership in AI for Science that we will look to grow and expand in the months and years ahead. Putting our advanced AI tools into the hands of American scientists Google DeepMind will provide an accelerated access program for scientists at all 17 DOE National Laboratories to our frontier AI for Science models and agentic tools, starting today with AI co-scientist on Google Cloud. AI co-scientist is a multi-agent virtual scientific collaborator built on Gemini, which is trained on Google's world class TPUs. This system is designed to help scientists synthesize vast amounts of information to generate novel hypotheses and research proposals, and accelerate the pace of scientific and biomedical discoveries. AI co-scientist is already showing its potential across diverse biomedical applications. It proposed novel drug repurposing candidates for liver fibrosis that were validated through laboratory experiments and predicted complex antimicrobial resistance mechanisms that matched experiments before they were even published, demonstrating the potential to accelerate hypothesis development from years to days. It’s also showing early promise in additional fields like physics, chemistry, computer science, and more. In early 2026, we will expand our accelerated access program for National Laboratories to include: AlphaEvolve - a Gemini-powered coding agent for designing advanced algorithms that is showing incredible promise for application across many areas in computing and math and, we believe, could be transformative across many more areas such as material science, drug discovery and energy. For example, AlphaEvolve enhanced the efficiency of Google's data centers, chip design and AI training processes — including training the large language models underlying AlphaEvolve itself. AlphaGenome - an AI model to help scientists better understand the non-coding part of DNA, speeding up research on genome biology and improving disease understanding. With more data on plant genomes, AlphaGenome could potentially be extended to help improve crop resistance and other applications including sustainable biofuels and advanced biomaterials. WeatherNext - a state-of-the-art family of weather forecasting models. Our partnership with the U.S. National Hurricane Center already supports their cyclone forecasts and warnings, helping communities prepare for disasters earlier. DOE and all National Laboratories can also access Gemini for Government , which brings together the best of Google’s AI-optimized and accredited commercial cloud with our industry-leading Gemini models - including our most intelligent model Gemini 3 with state-of-the-art reasoning capabilities and multimodal understanding. We’re excited to see what America’s leading researchers will be able to do with our frontier AI models and agentic tools. A history of collaboration for scientific progress We've seen what’s possible when industry-leading technology can build upon the work of the National Laboratories. The foundational work by DOE's Brookhaven National Laboratory on the Protein Data Bank was crucial for the development of AlphaFold, our AI system that can predict the 3D structure of proteins, the development of which was recognized through Demis Hassabis and John Jumper’s co-award of the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. The AlphaFold Protein Database has now been used by more than three million scientists in over 190 countries to accelerate research, from effective malaria vaccines to groundbreaking gene therapies. Looking ahead Through the Genesis Mission, we'll be accelerating American scientific leadership by also exploring research collaborations with National Laboratories in areas including fusion energy , new materials discovery and earth science . The challenges facing our world—from energy to disease to security—demand unprecedented scientific innovation. By combining human ingenuity with advanced AI capabilities, we believe we can help America's scientists achieve discoveries that would have seemed impossible just years ago. items.title: Anthropic’s IPO filing reveals its strategy for keeping enterprise customers hooked
items.description: Anthropic’s S-1 shows more than half of its $100,000-plus customers now use both the Claude Platform and a first-party app, a cross-selling playbook reminiscent of Amazon that’s making enterprise customers stickier.
items.content: Anthropic is building the same kind of cross-product ecosystem that helped make tech companies like Amazon and Uber enormously sticky, and its S-1 suggests the strategy is working. More than half of customers spending at least $100,000 annually now use both the Claude platform and a first-party app like Claude Code or Cowork, up from about 30% at the end of last year. “The speed and depth of our enterprise customer adoption are powerful evidence of Claude’s position at the frontier of AI,” the S-1, filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission on Monday , reads. As of September 30, Anthropic recorded more than 11,900 customers spending at least $100,000; more than 1,900 customers spending upward of $1 million; and about 250 customers spending $10 million or more annually. Anthropic attributes customer momentum to a “significant usage expansion as customers realize the value of deploying Claude across their organizations,” which drove net revenue retention of about 900% as of the end of the third quarter. Throwing shade at the entire legacy SaaS industry, Anthropic pitches Claude as not a “static product that serves a single use case,” but rather “frontier AI with rapidly advancing capabilities” spanning the models, the developer platform, and the applications users interact with directly. “An advance at any layer compounds across all three layers, accelerating the pace at which we can deliver more capable intelligence,” the filing reads, calling this “integrated approach” the reason more customers use both the Claude Platform and first-party apps. The playbook is familiar. Uber began by selling rides but has expanded into food delivery and freight. With AWS, Amazon drew in customers with cloud computing services before expanding those relationships into storage, databases, and other offerings, making the ecosystem increasingly hard to leave. Like those companies, Anthropic doesn’t have to sell each product to a brand-new buyer: A business that starts with the API can deploy Claude Code to their engineers and then Cowork to their broader workforce. Those app users become far more valuable. In the third quarter, the highest-spending 5% of Claude Enterprise customers who used Claude Code spent about 20x as much per month as the average enterprise user who didn’t use the coding tool, per the filing. The finding demonstrates how much room there is for per-user spend to grow, and illustrates why Anthropic is keen to get its applications into the accounts that start with the API. Anthropic said it amplifies that organic diffusion by investing in Applied AI teams. An internal Applied AI team works with startups and enterprises to help place Claude inside customers’ existing technology stacks, and the company recently launched a separate venture with Blackstone and other private equity firms, dubbed Ode with Anthropic, to embed forward-deployed engineers into businesses to build bespoke AI tools with Claude. Anthropic also leans on its third-party distribution partnerships with hyperscalers AWS, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure. Under what the filing calls a “joint go-to-market approach,” Anthropic holds the direct contractual relationship with customers and pays each cloud provider a fee, which the company says lets it “avoid channel conflict” and “set pricing.” Anthropic’s budding stickiness strategy may become essential as the AI giant seeks to constantly “reinvent our business” by releasing “new classes of products whose aim is to dwarf the economic value of our existing ones.” The company says it will devote less effort than a typical business to “entrenching our current products and business models, and more effort to defining new ones.” The filing also flags headwinds, despite impressive revenue growth of $16.3 billion for the first half of 2026, up from $1.2 billion in the same period last year. The cloud partnerships that help sell Claude are increasingly seeing Anthropic as a competitor, which Anthropic says could lead to difficulties securing the compute it needs from them. The filing states that Amazon, Google, and Microsoft may prioritize their own requirements or rivals they’ve invested in. Customer concentration is another risk. “Any adverse change in demand from our largest customers … could adversely affect our business and prospects,” reads part of the risk factors section. “As a result, a significant reduction in spending by, or the loss of, one or more of our largest customers, if not offset by new customer relationships or increased business from our other existing customers, could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.” Anthropic did not immediately respond to TechCrunch’s request for comment. items.title: Bringing foundational models to the front lines of TB screening
items.description: Generative AI
items.content: Bringing foundational models to the front lines of TB screening October 23, 2026 Preeti Singh, Lead, Technical Program Manager, and Shravya Shetty, Distinguished Software Engineer, Google Research Tuberculosis remains one of the world's deadliest infectious diseases, claiming an estimated 1.23 million lives each year. Despite decades of global investment, too many cases go undetected in the communities that carry the highest burden. Over the past five years, we’ve worked to change that trajectory, moving from early research benchmarks toward open foundation models that could be tuned and deployed at the point of care. Quick links Share Getting access to timely healthcare often comes down to an accident of geography: where you live, what resources your local clinic possesses, and whether a specialist is within reach. Nowhere is this disparity more acute than in the fight against tuberculosis (TB). Despite being preventable and curable, TB claims more than 1.23 million lives annually. A primary bottleneck is radiology: For those in high-burden settings, from people who live in remote rural areas to miners working deep underground, radiologists are scarce, and imaging infrastructure is often days away. As a result, millions of active cases go undetected, perpetuating transmission. Over the past several years, our team across Google Research and Google for Health has worked to change that trajectory: moving from an AI-based tool that builds on our existing work in medical imaging to identify people with presumptive TB for follow-up testing to prospective clinical trials, regulatory clearance with local partners, and ultimately open foundation models like MedGemma that empower public health systems worldwide. This week at IDWeek 2026 in Washington, D.C., we are sharing how we’re bringing health AI research to reality, and how foundational models can democratize TB screening at global scale. Proving AI-based tools can read chest radiographs Our work began with a fundamental question: Can AI-based tools interpret chest radiographs (CXRs) with the accuracy of an expert radiologist for TB screening? Chest radiography is the frontline imaging modality for pulmonary screening, but detecting subtle signs of TB like apical infiltrates (fluid in the top portion of the lung) and cavitary lesions (tissue damage) requires specialized expertise that is rarely available in rural clinics. In 2019, we published a benchmark in Radiology , demonstrating that deep learning algorithms could detect active pulmonary TB at performance levels matching experienced radiologists. Real-world utility, however, demands independent verification. In August 2021, the Stop TB Partnership evaluated automated computer-aided detection (CAD) software across diverse patient cohorts in The Lancet Digital Health , ranking our model among the top-performing TB screening algorithms globally. That year, WHO also recommended CAD for TB screening and triage. In September 2024, in NEJM AI , we detailed a prospective, multi-site validation demonstrating that AI-assisted screening maintains high sensitivity (minimizing missed cases) across diverse patient populations, while also reliably detecting other incidental pulmonary and cardiac abnormalities. Navigating the translation gap In medical AI, publishing a paper is only the beginning. Between an algorithmic model and a trusted bedside tool lies the "translation gap": making software reliable across varied X-ray machines and offline settings, integrating it into clinical workflows, and meeting medical device regulations. With this in mind, we partnered with Nexus AI , a Pretoria-based medical technology company, and they translated our chest X-ray algorithms into a certified clinical diagnostic tool. Navigating the regulatory landscape required extensive audits: CE MDR class IIb certification : Under the European Union’s Medical Device Regulation ( EU MDR 2017/745 ), Nexus AI achieved Class IIb certification — a rigorous designation that verifies the tool is safe for real-world patient care based on prospective clinical evaluations. Quality standards : Nexus AI obtained certified compliance with ISO 13485 for medical device quality management. Global access : Nexus AI signed an agreement with FIND to pursue the World Health Organization Pre-qualification (WHO PQ) , which is essential for international procurement through global agencies, alongside an ongoing pathway toward the U.S. FDA clearance . The Nexus AI device screens chest X-rays for lung diseases like TB in as little as 45 seconds. Frontline impact: Reaching patients where they are Today, Nexus Intelligence is actively deploying this technology where diagnostic access is most urgently needed. Across six countries — South Africa, Sierra Leone, and Côte d'Ivoire, with expansions underway in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Zambia, and Cameroon — Nexus AI’s tool operates in approximately 40 healthcare facilities. To date, over 90 clinicians have evaluated more than 25,000 chest radiographs , reducing turnaround times from weeks to under 45 seconds, accelerating rapid triage while empowering healthcare professionals to make final clinical decisions. Our collaboration commits to health equity: Nexus AI has delivered more than 3,000 free screenings to under-resourced public clinics, progressing toward a goal of 10,000 sponsored screenings annually . Screening at the extremes: The Mponeng Gold Mine Perhaps no deployment better illustrates meeting patients where they are than the work done at the Mponeng Gold Mine in South Africa, one of the deepest mines in the world. Deep-shaft miners face chronic silica dust exposure and an elevated risk of pulmonary disease . In partnership with the Stop TB Partnership , Harmony Gold Mine , and the South African Department of Health , Nexus AI deployed ultra-portable digital X-ray kits and offline AI four kilometers underground. Miners are screened on-site within seconds, and those flagged with presumptive TB can be immediately referred for confirmatory molecular testing. Screening, triage and confirmatory testing can now happen in a single visit, compressing a pathway that often takes weeks. From point solution to open foundations: HAI-DEF and MedGemma A custom solution with a single partner cannot address the global TB burden alone. To scale impact, we shifted from isolated deployments to building open, adaptable foundations that allow developers and health ministries to create solutions tailored to local needs. Through the Health AI Developer Foundations (HAI-DEF), we open-sourced our chest X-ray embeddings and MedSigLIP , a lightweight vision-language model trained to align medical images, such as chest X-rays, with the clinical language used to describe them. Because MedSigLIP understands both images and text, developers can use it to classify or search images with plain-language labels, or fine-tune it for a specific task with only a small set of local examples. This lets local teams build specialized models on modest regional datasets and reach strong performance without massive compute resources. Building on this, we released MedGemma , a family of open-weight multimodal models (4B and 27B parameter configurations). MedGemma advances from basic classification to multimodal clinical reasoning: it synthesizes radiographic findings with clinical history, answers clinician queries in natural language, and runs locally on-device without internet access. Since its launch, MedGemma has seen more than 10 million downloads worldwide. Nexus AI’s application analyzes a chest X-ray integrating models, which highlights findings that are not consistent with normal lung fields, including findings suggestive of tuberculosis, and when further investigation is required (FIR) . Sovereign scale: Supporting Indonesia’s national TB initiative Open models help enable public health systems to build sovereign solutions that protect patient privacy. In Southeast Asia, the Ministry of Health of Indonesia is addressing the world's second-highest TB burden with an ambitious goal: screening 50 million citizens annually to eradicate the disease. Reviewing 50 million X-rays manually is infeasible, and proprietary cloud software poses data residency challenges. Instead, the Ministry is fine-tuning MedGemma and MedSigLIP on domestic chest radiographs . Because the models run on local infrastructure, patient data remains within national borders, giving health leaders full sovereignty over clinical deployment. Complementary screening: Bioacoustics with HeAR Recognizing that imaging equipment cannot reach every remote health post, Google Research also developed Health Acoustic Representations (HeAR) . Trained on over 300 million audio segments , HeAR enables non-invasive acoustic screening from cough sounds recorded on a standard smartphone microphone . HeAR is being utilized through collaborative research across sub-Saharan Africa with CIDRZ (Zambia), the Aurum Institute (Ghana, supported by a $250,000 Google.org grant), and HELINA ’s $1.5 million regional collaborative. Together, acoustic triage (HeAR), mobile X-ray screening (HAI-DEF), and multimodal clinical reasoning (MedGemma) offer communities an integrated diagnostic cascade of tools for underserved populations. Looking ahead The journey from a laboratory algorithm to a CE-certified tool used in clinics across six countries has shown us what it takes to turn research into real-world impact: rigorous science, open developer platforms, and dedicated local partnerships. Because our partners know their communities best, they are now taking this work further. Nexus AI is expanding to new countries, Indonesia is integrating TB screening into its national program, and CIDRZ, the Aurum Institute and HELINA are building the clinical evidence for cough-based triage. Our role is to help equip them with open models, foundational research and ongoing support, so that more people with TB are diagnosed and treated sooner. At IDWeek 2026, we look forward to connecting with the infectious disease and public health communities as we work together to expand equitable care. Acknowledgements We thank our collaborators at Nexus AI , Stop TB Partnership , UNOPS , CIDRZ , Aurum Institute , HELINA , Harmony Gold Mine , the South African Department of Health , and the Indonesian Ministry of Health for their clinical leadership and dedication to global health equity. items.title: Does Your Model Run on AWS Trainium? Look It Up
items.content: Back to Articles a]:hidden"> Does Your Model Run on AWS Trainium? Look It Up Published October 23, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 29 +23 David Corvoysier dacorvo Follow :last-child]:mb-0"> In a previous post , we introduced TorchNeuron, the native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium (the torch-neuronx package). With it, Transformers runs its own modeling code on Trainium, as it does on any other device, so any Transformers model on the Hub may run. Which ones actually do? The torch-neuronx model support Space answers that question for the most popular models on the Hub. It tells you whether a model runs unmodified on Trainium, and gives you the script to run it yourself. Look up a model The Space opens on the Selected view: our own selection of models picked among the top models on the Hub by downloads and by trending score. Each row gives the result, the number of Trainium cores the model is sharded over, the wall time of the run (compilation included) and the peak device memory. To look up a given model, switch to the Trending or Downloads view and type part of its name. These views follow the Hub's own rankings, one task at a time, whether a model was tested or not. When a model was left out on purpose, the Space tells you why (most of the time it was not prioritized, sometimes it is truly incompatible). You can also pick the versions of the Neuron compiler ( neuronx-cc ) and of Transformers to look at. At the time of writing, only Transformers models are tested, and our selection is limited to text-generation and image-text-to-text models. We plan to expand to diffusers, sentence transformers, and other transformers tasks. Run it yourself Select a model to see how to run it. The Space lists the Neuron stack the model was tested on, the packages to install on top of it, and the run.py script that ran. The script follows the recipe of the TorchNeuron announcement : it loads the model with from_pretrained , sharded when it needs to be, then generates with a static cache and torch.compile(backend="neuron") . On a Trainium2 ( trn2 ) instance with that stack, for example in the AWS Neuron Deep Learning Container , install the packages, then run: python3 run.py No need for torchrun : the script launches its own torch.distributed ranks when the model is sharded. A first run starts by compiling the model's graphs. To skip that step, copy the graphs the same compiler built during the test, from the public NEFF cache bucket. The Space gives you the command, with the right compiler version: hf buckets sync hf://buckets/aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-neff-cache/neuronxcc-<version> /tmp/neff_cache What "runs" means Each test loads the model on a trn2 instance, sharded over the smallest number of Trainium cores that can hold its weights. Most models are sharded with tensor parallelism. Mixture-of-experts models without a tensor-parallel plan use expert parallelism only. The test then generates 32 tokens and checks them. On a single core, the tokens are compared with those of a CPU run of the same checkpoint. When the model is sharded, a small judge model checks that the text is fluent English. At the time of writing, only models that fit on 4 Trainium2 devices are tested, which means 16 cores at most. A PASS says nothing about throughput, or about longer generations. The results are a dataset Everything the Space shows comes from the public aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-model-support dataset, with one Parquet file per pair of neuronx-cc and library versions. Each row holds a model's result, the error when it failed, the versions of the whole stack and the run.py that ran. You can query it directly: import pandas as pd df = pd.read_parquet( "hf://datasets/aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-model-support/data" ) df[df.model_id == "Qwen/Qwen3-0.6B" ][[ "neuronx_cc" , "library" , "library_version" , "neuron_cores" , "result" ]] The dataset card gives the exact meaning of each result. Next time you wonder whether a model runs on Trainium, look it up . items.title: Turning Database Grading into RL Rewards: Post-Training Agents with ThinkingBox
items.content: Back to Articles a]:hidden"> Turning Database Grading into RL Rewards: Post-Training Agents with ThinkingBox Enterprise Article Published October 22, 2026 Upvote 22 +16 Tuhin Kundu tuhink Follow microsoft :last-child]:mb-0"> This is the follow up to our first blog post, The Agent Said It Was Done. The Database Disagreed. ThinkingBox-Training is now available on GitHub . We built ThinkingBox to evaluate an agent's work by comparing the final database state with the expected outcome. We then used the same kind of executable signal as a reward on training tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench. For Qwen3.8-27B, average success rose from 51.70% to 60.78%, while tasks completed correctly on all twenty attempts rose from 38 to 107 with 50 GRPO steps. Figure 1. ThinkingBox turns executable checks of terminal database state into rewards for post-training agents on tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench. This is a joint blog by Microsoft and Hugging Face, special thanks to Mirco Milletari and Xiang Jiang from Microsoft, Sergio Paniego from Hugging Face and our former intern Zhuochun Li (University of Pittsburgh) for co-authoring/reviewing efforts. We built ThinkingBox to catch agents that say they are done when they are not. Each of its 507 tasks in ThinkingBox-Bench (our benchmark dataset) hands an agent a real backend and a set of tools, lets it work, then checks what really changed in the database. In the first post , we caught a model closing a customer's ticket as resolved while the carrier exception behind it was still open. Nine competent-looking tool calls, one wrong database row. Then we noticed what we had built. For most tasks, an executable check can return 1 or 0 directly from the final database state. That is not just a grader. This can be a reward function. + So we constructed a training pool from ThinkingBox-format tasks outside the benchmark and used their executable outcomes as rewards. The catch was choosing which tasks are suitable for agent training: most tasks are either already solved or hopeless for the model in front of you, and both teach it nothing. Difficulty is policy-relative: a task is hard for the current model only until that model learns it. We call this offline policy-relative difficulty . We estimated each task's success probability once using the base policy before training and kept the selected training pool fixed throughout the run. What happened after training We used offline policy-relative difficulty to build the training pool, then fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B with GRPO for 50 steps. To recap, we evaluate each of the 507 benchmark tasks 20 times. pass@1 measures average success across all 10,140 attempts. pass@20 measures the share of tasks solved at least once. Observed 20/20 measures the share of tasks that pass every recorded attempt. Table 1. Qwen3.8-27B results before and after 50 steps of GRPO on the offline-selected training pool. Metric Base RL fine-tuned Change Observed 20/20 38 (7.50%) → 107 (21.10%) +69 tasks pass@1 (successful attempts) 5,242 (51.70%) → 6,163 (60.78%) +9.08 pt pass@20 (tasks solved at least once) 453 (89.35%) → 446 (87.97%) −7 tasks Training sharply increased repeatable success, with a small decline in at-least-once coverage. The rest of the post explains how we selected practice tasks, built the reward loop, and measured that tradeoff. What does that improvement look like on one task? A traveler requests a room downgrade, but company policy requires manager approval first. Before training, the agent changed the booking and issued refunds without approval in 15 of 20 attempts. After RL fine-tuning, it preserved the booking and payment state in all 20. Figure 2. One corporate hotel-booking task, 20 attempts per model. The base Qwen3.8-27B model changed the booking without required manager approval in 15 attempts. The RL fine-tuned model preserved booking and payment state in all 20; all expected records matched in 19. Contents What the benchmark found, in sixty seconds Results: the dependability column moved Where the gains landed What dependability costs The training loop Offline policy-relative difficulty What earns a reward Run the training stack Where this goes next In a hurry? The headline result is above. The implementation is in Run the training stack . What the benchmark found, in sixty seconds ThinkingBox-Bench grades agents on the database records they leave behind. Each of its 507 tasks starts a real backend, hands the agent a set of MCP tools and a simulated LLM user with private context, and at the end runs executable checks against the terminal database state. Checks are against the backend record that needs to be correct, not the specific tool calls. This incentivizes the model to discover possibly new solution paths rather than “rediscover” the human-backed solution, that might be suboptimal albeit correct. In our first post we ran eighteen models through that benchmark twenty times each and reported a gap that headline accuracy hides. Kimi-K3 solved 93.89% of tasks at least once but completed only 68 of 507 tasks (13.41%) on all twenty recorded attempts . Claude Opus 5 inverted it: narrower coverage, far more consistency. And bigger or better model did not close it. Claude Opus 5.5 scored 0.66 percentage points higher than Claude Opus 5 on pass@1, yet passed exactly the same number of tasks, 241 , on all twenty attempts. That gain in headline accuracy bought zero additional dependability. If you are choosing a model for work that touches production database records, pass@1 should not be read alone. Observed 20/20 shows which tasks succeed on every attempt, which is closer to what production reliability requires. The executable terminal-state verdict was also the training reward. Before unpacking the training loop, here is what changed on the sealed benchmark. Results: the dependability column moved After training Qwen3.8-27B, we evaluated the selected step-50 checkpoint on the 507-task benchmark it had never trained on. The 507 tasks represent an out-of-distribution test set: their domains, databases, and most MCP tools were not encountered during RL training. Table 2. ThinkingBox-Bench pass@1 (%) by domain, for selected models from our first blog's Table 2 and our fine-tuned model for different domains and overall. Observed 20/20 numbers are over the entire benchmark with 507 tasks. Each model is evaluated on all 507 tasks for 20 repeated trials. Bold marks the column leader; underline marks the runner-up. Model Retail Auto insurance Travel Neobank Consulting Overall Observed 20/20 Claude Opus 5.5 80.97 68.40 54.28 71.25 61.58 67.16 241 (47.53%) Claude Opus 5 80.71 65.80 49.95 70.62 66.19 66.50 241 (47.53%) GPT-5.4 76.33 62.65 68.12 65.34 54.60 65.36 128 (25.25%) GPT-5.6 Sol 67.65 65.30 60.34 59.09 57.52 61.91 82 (16.17%) Qwen3.8-27B RLFT 67.91 56.45 62.69 62.40 54.51 60.78 107 (21.10%) Claude Sonnet 4.6 72.35 54.40 58.94 56.39 54.31 59.19 102 (20.12%) GPT-6 Astra 71.73 46.55 55.87 60.87 56.83 58.31 231 (45.56%) Kimi-K3 82.24 50.80 61.83 41.35 51.63 57.37 68 (13.41%) Qwen3.8-27B 64.03 47.85 53.41 47.88 45.69 51.70 38 (7.50%) The headline result is the observed-20/20 row in Table 1. A 27B model that initially completed 38 (7.5%) of ThinkingBox-Bench on every attempt now completes 107 (21.1%) on every attempt, almost thrice. For comparison, observed 20/20 for Kimi-K3 is 68, GPT-5.4 with 128, GPT-6 Astra has 231, and Claude Opus 5.5 leads with 241. Average success and repeatability produce different orderings. In Table 2, we notice that GPT-5.6 Sol scored slightly higher on pass@1 than the RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B (61.91% versus 60.78%) but passed fewer tasks on all 20 recorded attempts: 82 versus 107. Claude Sonnet 4.6 scored lower on pass@1, at 59.19%, yet passed nearly the same number of tasks every time, at 102. Neither metric alone captures the full picture. The observed pattern is consistent with sharpening: repeatable success rose while at-least-once coverage fell slightly. This is in-line with prior work . One explanation is that probability distribution moved toward trajectories that work repeatedly while some low-probability paths disappeared. Overall, the model did not become broader. It became more repeatable. The next question is where those gains landed. Where the gains landed Figure 3. Domain-level base scores, RLFT scores, and percentage-point changes. Green change cells show gains and red cells show declines; blue shading indicates the score level within each metric. Pass@1 and observed 20/20 rose in all five domains. Pass@20 was mixed: it increased in neobank and consulting, but declined in retail, travel, and auto insurance. Auto insurance had the largest breadth loss (−7.0 points), while retail had the largest observed-20/20 gain (+24.5 points). What dependability costs The first post priced consistency using simple math: divide the estimated cost of the full 20-run campaign by the number of tasks the model passed every single time. Cost per dependable task = estimated cost of the 507 × 20 campaign ÷ tasks passing 20/20 Applying the same cost math to the fine-tuned checkpoint's measured token usage: Table 3. Estimated evaluation cost and dependability for base and RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B. Cost per successful attempt divides total estimated campaign cost (507 x 20) by the number of passing attempts. Measure Base RL fine-tuned Change Campaign cost, 20 runs $925.80 → $855.58 −7.6% Cost per successful attempt $0.177 → $0.139 −21.4% Tasks passing 20/20 38 → 107 2.8× as many Cost per dependable task $24.36 → $8.00 −67.2% At $8.00 per dependable task, the fine-tuned model came close to GPT-5.4 ($6.80), GPT-6 Astra ($7.45), and Claude Opus 5.5 ($7.80) in the companion comparison. The single-attempt view Figure 4 prices cost per successful attempt against pass@1. Figure 4. The golden arrow traces Qwen3.8-27B base pareto cost position to the RLFT (diamond): pass@1 rises from 51.70% to 60.78% while estimated cost per successful attempt falls from $0.177 to $0.139. Ringed circles mark the Pareto cost frontier. The move places the fine-tuned checkpoint close to GPT-5.6 Sol, although GPT-5.6 Sol remains cheaper and slightly higher on pass@1. Four models priced in our paper fall outside the plotted range. The dollar values are a comparative serving index, not invoice or cloud bills. Serving the fine-tuned checkpoint would be the same as the base model. The calculation includes model inference cost, and excludes training run and policy-probe cost for curating the training dataset. These results tell us what moved. The next sections explain the training loop and why selecting the right tasks matters the most. The training loop Figure 5. The six stages, now in context: candidate tasks feed in, the first three run once offline, the last three repeat for every group in the training run. The trained checkpoint is evaluated against ThinkingBox-Bench. Selection runs once, offline, against the base policy model, i.e in this case Qwen3.8 27B; training then uses that fixed pool that has been curated. The dashed amber arrow in Figure 5 marks the path we did not take: re-probing difficulty during the training run. Every rollout is a complete episode, not a text completion. It gets a fresh backend, an isolated MCP session, and GPT-5 Chat as the simulated user. Most rewards come from deterministic terminal-state checks; a minority of narrow rubric requirements can invoke the configured judge (GPT-5 Chat). Training and evaluation must interpret Qwen output identically. That includes reasoning extraction, tool calls, argument typing, rendering, and isolated task state. Otherwise the reward measures a different agent from the one evaluated. The shared interpretation code is in trainer/core/tb_interpret.py . For the reference run, we ran full-parameter RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B on 187 tasks using token-mean GRPO. Each update generated 18 groups of 8 rollouts, or 144 episodes, across 24 H100s. Training ran synchronously with parameter and optimizer offload; AdamW used a 1e-6 learning rate and zero weight decay. We ran the training for 50 steps. Zero-variance groups were replaced DAPO-style during training. System errors were handled separately: a backend timeout is not an incorrect agent outcome, so affected groups were refilled rather than scored as failures. That explains how retained tasks were trained. The remaining question is which tasks entered the training pool. Offline policy-relative difficulty Before diving deep into the selection of training tasks, a disclaimer: No ThinkingBox-Bench task was included in the RL training pool. The benchmark was reserved for evaluation. ThinkingBox-Bench is out-of-distribution relative to the RL training pool: its domains, databases, policies, and most tools were not encountered during RL training. The two sets still share the ThinkingBox framework, simulated-user machinery, executable terminal-state grading, a few common tools, and a similar task style. These shared elements limit the scope of the transfer claim. Why selection matters comes down to one arithmetic fact about GRPO. If all eight rollouts fail, the reward vector is [0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0] . If all eight succeed, it is [1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1] . In either case, centering within the group produces no task-reward advantage because no trajectory did better than another. ++ A mixed group such as [0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1] supplies the contrast GRPO can learn from. That distinction is expensive for a stateful agent: every rollout provisions an isolated backend, runs a real tool session, and calls a separate model to play the user. The question that shaped this work was therefore not only which model or optimizer? It was: which candidate tasks should enter the fixed training pool? We used an offline pass-rate filter on the posterior to select the training pool. It estimates which tasks are likely to produce contrasting terminal rewards under the base policy. So we probe. Each candidate task is run repeatedly against the base policy model. The plain-language rule is simple: tasks the model always fails are unlikely to teach it yet; tasks it always passes are already learned; tasks it solves sometimes are where outcomes can provide contrast. Estimating difficulty from limited probes Each candidate task is run n times, producing k successes. We model its latent success probability with Jeffreys posterior probability: success probability | k successes in n probes ~ Beta(k + ½, n − k + ½) Figure 6. Offline policy-relative difficulty is estimated from repeated base-policy probes and used to retain tasks likely to produce contrasting rewards. We partition the unit interval into five buckets with boundaries at 0.08, 0.40, 0.60, and 0.90, chosen as hyperparameters for these runs. Each task is assigned to the bucket containing the greatest posterior mass: Rarely solved [0, 0.08): drop Difficult [0.08, 0.40): keep Intermediate [0.40, 0.60): keep Frequently solved [0.60, 0.90): keep for full-parameter RLFT Nearly always solved [0.90, 1]: drop Further details are in Appendix C.4 of our ThinkingBox paper . One task, end to end Figure 7. Zooming in, one task through all six stages: GPT-5.4 screening, base-model probes, difficulty classification, a rollout group, terminal-state grading, and a GRPO update. Figure 7 follows one candidate task that can potentially enter the training pool. For the Qwen3.8 27B full-parameter pool, GPT-5.4 first served as a solvability screen. The base policy then succeeded on few of the probes e.g 3 of 8, producing a Beta(3.5, 5.5) posterior. Its largest mass, 54.0%, fell in the Difficult band. When sampled for training, the task produced the mixed reward group [0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1] . Successful trajectories therefore received above-mean task advantage and failed trajectories below-mean advantage, giving GRPO contrast to learn from. A different policy model could place the same task in a different difficulty band. The final Qwen3.8-27B curated training pool contained 187 tasks. What earns a reward Nothing about the trajectory. The reward is the task's own executable verdict. When an episode ends, the sandbox extracts what actually changed in the backend and runs the task's deterministic checks against the terminal state. Any trajectory that produces the correct end state passes. Wrong, missing, or extra side effects fail. The reward is 1 or 0. In the benchmark, the database grader can be thought of as the “examiner”: it caught agents that reported success and left the wrong record. In training, the same kind of check can be seen as the “teacher” on a different, disjoint set of tasks. Two reward paths, one binary verdict Executable check (the large majority). When the required outcome is represented in terminal state or side effects, a deterministic test accepts or rejects it; no LLM judge call is needed. Judge-assisted check (a minority). When a narrow requirement cannot be determined cleanly from database state, the configured LLM judge answers a binary rubric question used by the executable test. Run the training stack We release the data-selection, rollout, reward, and Verl integration used to train Qwen3.8-27B in microsoft/thinkingbox-training . The repository README is the entry point. The detailed guides are: docs/data-preparation.md for task hydration, policy probes, benchmark exclusion, and train/validation splitting; docs/reference-q38-run.md for the validated 24-H100 Qwen3.8 configuration; docs/evaluation.md for merging a checkpoint and running ThinkingBox-Bench 507 x 20. Before you start Tested on Linux and WSL with Python 3.12 and uv . You need NVIDIA GPUs with a compatible CUDA/NCCL stack, a local Qwen3.8-27B checkpoint, and OpenAI-compatible endpoints for the simulated user and judge. The validated reference configuration uses 3 nodes x 8 H100 GPUs; smaller custom configurations depend on model size, context length, and rollout concurrency. The public sample task list exercises the interface. It is not the private 187-task training pool used for the reported run. Supply an authorized training source that remains disjoint from the public benchmark. Install Keep the three repositories side by side: mkdir -p ~/thinkingbox-workspace cd ~/thinkingbox-workspace git clone https://github.com/microsoft/thinkingbox.git git clone https://github.com/microsoft/thinkingbox-data.git git clone --branch main https://github.com/microsoft/thinkingbox-training git -C thinkingbox checkout 892964e7226044e5463ad188da119df838f4bec1 git -C thinkingbox-data checkout thinkingbox-bench-v1.0 Create the validated environment The released stack targets Linux, Python 3.12, Verl 0.9.0, and the pinned package lock: cd ~/thinkingbox-workspace/thinkingbox-training uv venv --python 3.12 source .venv/bin/activate uv sync --frozen --extra fast --extra tracking --extra eval-proxy uv pip install -e ../thinkingbox uv pip install --config-settings editable-mode=compat \ -e ../thinkingbox-data/servers/thinkingbox_tools uv pip install --config-settings editable-mode=compat \ -e ../thinkingbox-data/servers/tb_business_ops_servers_202606 python scripts/prepare_verl.py --dest .deps/verl --install python scripts/verify_verl_install.py uv pip check The final two commands should report a verified patched Verl checkout and no broken requirements. Do not run another automatic package sync afterward: it can replace the patched source installation with the vanilla Verl wheel. Prepare the training data Start with the publicly provided samples, or add your own authorized dataset in ThinkingBox format. Then run the repository's preparation script: cd ~/thinkingbox-workspace/thinkingbox-training source .venv/bin/activate python data/prepare_data.py -- help The script aggregates policy probes, applies offline policy-relative difficulty filters and benchmark exclusions, and writes the selected train.yaml and test.yaml files. docs/data-preparation.md documents the input fields, loader contract, and complete command. Configure and inspect the launch Follow docs/reference-q38-run.md to start Typesense and the MCP servers, configure the simulated user and judge, set the model, task-list, checkpoint, and topology variables, and prepare the Ray cluster. Keep credentials in runtime secret injection rather than committed files or shell history. Before allocating a training job, use the guide's dry-run command: DRY_RUN= true ./scripts/run_train.sh \ trainer.total_training_steps=50 \ trainer.save_freq=5 It must exit zero without starting Ray or allocating GPUs. Read the emitted python -m verl.trainer.main_ppo command and every resolved override before launching the run. Train The launcher configures training; it does not provision hosts. On the reference three-node topology, export the same environment on every node, mount CHECKPOINT_DIR at the same absolute path, then start Ray: # head node ROLE= head NODE_IP= " $HEAD_IP " GPUS_PER_NODE=8 \ ./scripts/start_ray.sh # each worker node ROLE=worker NODE_IP= " $WORKER_IP " \ HEAD_ADDRESS= " $HEAD_IP :6379" GPUS_PER_NODE=8 \ ./scripts/start_ray.sh After ray status reports all 24 GPUs, launch once from the head node: export RAY_ADDRESS=auto export GPUS=0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7 ./scripts/run_train.sh \ trainer.project_name=thinkingbox-training \ trainer.experiment_name=q38-full-rlft \ trainer.total_training_steps=50 \ trainer.save_freq=5 Evaluate the checkpoint through OpenEnv The first ThinkingBox post covers Typesense, the MCP Session Proxy, and OpenEnv setup. Merge the trained checkpoint following docs/evaluation.md , then serve it with vLLM. From the OpenEnv repository root, set MERGED_MODEL to the merged model directory and THINKINGBOX_DATA to the pinned benchmark checkout. The historical checkpoint evaluation used this eight-A100 serving configuration: vllm serve " $MERGED_MODEL " \ --served-model-name q38-rlft \ --host 127.0.0.1 \ --port 8001 \ --tensor-parallel-size 8 \ --dtype bfloat16 \ --max-model-len 262144 \ --gpu-memory-utilization 0.85 \ --max-num-seqs 16 \ --max-num-batched-tokens 8192 \ --language-model-only \ --enable-chunked-prefill \ --enable-prefix-caching \ --reasoning-parser qwen3 \ --enable-auto-tool-choice \ --tool-call-parser qwen3_xml In a separate terminal, start the OpenEnv compatibility proxy for the Qwen chat template from the ThinkingBox Training checkout. It listens on port 8014 and forwards to vLLM on 8001: cd ~/thinkingbox-workspace/thinkingbox-training source .venv/bin/activate bash scripts/launch_sysmerge.sh Keep it running during evaluation. From another terminal, check readiness: curl --fail http://127.0.0.1:8014/readyz Update the agent entry in the existing thinkingbox.yaml ; retain its MCP, simulated-user, and judge configuration: orchestrator: agent_model: type: aoai endpoint_url: http://127.0.0.1:8014/v1/chat/completions deployment: q38-rlft credential: type: api-key api_key: <your_api_key> is_reasoning: true temperature: 1.0 top_k: 20 top_p: 0.95 max_completion_tokens: 8192 timeout: 1800 Start OpenEnv as in the first post, with OPENENV_TB_CONFIG pointing to this thinkingbox.yaml and OPENENV_TB_DATASET to $THINKINGBOX_DATA . Once /ready succeeds, run the full protocol of 507 tasks × 20 attempts: uv run --project envs/thinkingbox_env --frozen \ thinkingbox-eval \ --config " $PWD /thinkingbox.yaml" \ --base-url http://127.0.0.1:8000 \ --dataset " $THINKINGBOX_DATA " \ --output q38-rlft-full.jsonl \ --errors-output q38-rlft-full-errors.jsonl \ --repeat 20 \ --coverage-profile full \ --aggregate-output q38-rlft-full-aggregate.json \ --message-timeout 1800 The full profile validates all 10,140 expected task/repetition keys before aggregation. Where this goes next The useful part of this work is not one Qwen3.8-27B checkpoint. It is the training loop and training data curation that turns executable outcomes into rewards. If you are training or evaluating an agent that touches real database records: Probe before you train. Take your own agent task set, run the base policy against it n times, and look at the band histogram. In our experience teams often have not inspected this distribution, and it is usually more lopsided than expected. Check your parity. Replay the same recorded model output through the training and evaluation parsers, and verify that both extract identical tool names and arguments. Otherwise, training may reward behavior that evaluation interprets differently. Report both coverage and repeatability. State how many tasks pass at least once in k attempts and how many pass all k . A model that occasionally finds a solution is not necessarily one that repeats it consistently. Further details can be found in the following links: Environment: envs/thinkingbox_env OpenEnv: ThinkingBox environment documentation Framework: microsoft/thinkingbox · tutorial Benchmark: microsoft/thinkingbox-data · v1.0 release Dataset viewer: microsoft/ThinkingBox-Bench Paper: arXiv:2608.19741 or HF RL training: microsoft/thinkingbox-training Blog: The Agent Said It Was Done. The Database Disagreed. Cite the paper @article{li2026thinkingbox, title = {One Success Isn't Reliability: Thinkingbox, a Sandbox and Benchmark for Agents in Stateful Business Workflows}, author = {Li, Zhuochun and Ko, Youngmin and Keramati, Ali and Kundu, Tuhin and Tsai, Liang-Chun and Ferri, Nicola and Milletari, Mirco and Liu, Jiaxiang and Lopez Pelaez, Susana Palmaz and Wang, Yuepeng and Smolyakov, Vadim and Jiang, Xiang and Olafsson, Kjartan and Guy, Tommy}, journal = {arXiv preprint arXiv:2608.19741}, year = {2026}, url = {https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.19741} } ThinkingBox code is MIT-licensed; the benchmark data is CDLA-Permissive-2.0 . Disclaimer: every task in the public benchmark is a synthetic reconstruction. The workflows and policies are modeled on real enterprise agent patterns; the customers are not real. ThinkingBox, ThinkingBox-Bench and ThinkingBox-Training is built by the Microsoft Copilot Studio team in partnership with Toloka with collaborators from the University of Pittsburgh, Northwestern University, Columbia University and UC Irvine who interned at Microsoft. Questions are welcome in the comments section below or on github or by email at firstnamelastname@microsoft.com . + A minority of tasks also include narrow binary rubric requirements for outcomes that the database cannot capture cleanly; those checks can invoke the configured LLM judge. ++ That zero-gradient problem has a standard batch-time fix: oversample, discard the degenerate groups, refill. The full-parameter run did exactly that, similar to DAPO with replacement of zero-variance groups. But refilling still pays full price for every wasted rollout before throwing it away. items.title: Ensemble forecasting with IBM Granite time-series models
items.content: Back to Articles a]:hidden"> Ensemble forecasting with IBM Granite time-series models Enterprise Article Published October 22, 2026 Upvote 24 +18 Fearghal O'Donncha Fearghal Follow ibm-research Chandramouli Kamanchi rry003 Follow ibm-research Guruprasad Ranjini Follow ibm-research Wesley M. Gifford wmgifford Follow ibm-research Natalia Martinez Gil natalialmg91 Follow ibm-research Bradley Eck bradleyjeck Follow ibm-research Pankaj Dayama pankajdayama Follow ibm-research Roman Vaculin vaculin Follow ibm-research Ayhan Sebin ayhansebin Follow ibm-research :last-child]:mb-0"> Four open Granite models, one extensible forecasting interface, and less guesswork about which model to use. Pre-trained time-series models can forecast without training on your dataset, but you still have to choose one. A model that handles smooth industrial signals well may struggle with noisy retail demand or a long seasonal horizon, and the best choice depends on the series and the task. Granite Timeseries Ensemble reduces that choice to a sensible default. One recipe combines four complementary Granite architectures and returns median and quantile forecasts, with no retraining and no fitted ensemble weights. Start with the Probabilistic Ensemble (uniform probability pooling), compare the adaptive Inter Quartile Range (IQR) Ensemble, and extend the same interface with compatible forecasters. The ensemble recipe and its default Granite members are permissively licensed. The idea will be familiar from weather forecasting. Ensemble forecasts explore a range of possible outcomes, and systems such as the North American Multi-Model Ensemble combine different models for seasonal prediction. Time-series forecasting benefits in a similar way: complementary models offer different views of what comes next, and an ensemble merges those views into one forecast. Try Granite Timeseries Ensemble Install Granite TSFM and load the recommended four-model recipe directly from Hugging Face: pip install "granite-tsfm>=0.3.11" import pandas as pd from tsfm_public.models.ensemble.modeling_ensemble import QuantileEnsembleForecaster df = pd.read_csv( "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/zhouhaoyi/ETDataset/main/ETT-small/ETTh1.csv" , parse_dates=[ "date" ], ) ensemble = QuantileEnsembleForecaster.from_pretrained( "ibm-granite/granite-timeseries-ensemble-r1" , ) result = ensemble( df.tail( 1024 ), timestamp_column= "date" , target_columns=[ "OT" ], context_length= 1024 , prediction_length= 24 , ) print (result.prediction_outputs) # point forecast print (result.quantile_outputs) # quantiles The recipe stores the ensemble configuration rather than merged model weights. It downloads the four member checkpoints at runtime, so allow extra time for the first run. For the full configuration, member checkpoints, evaluation details, and limitations, see the model card . result.prediction_outputs contains the point forecast, while result.quantile_outputs contains the quantile predictions which by default range from 0.1 to 0.9. Applications can use the point value as a central prediction and selected quantiles to express forecast ranges. For example, the 0.1 and 0.9 quantiles define a central forecast interval with nominal 80% coverage. The ensemble members The default recipe combines four pre-trained Granite models with different architectures: Model Architecture Granite PatchTST-FM-r1 Patched Transformer Granite PatchTST-FM-r2 Patched Conformer Granite FlowState-r1.1 State-space model Granite TTM-r3 Tiny Time Mixers (MLP mixer) For background, see the PatchTST-FM-r1 paper , PatchTST-FM-r2 architecture overview , FlowState paper , and Tiny Time Mixers paper . These architectures capture trends, seasonality, and local variation in different ways, so their errors need not coincide. A 50-year review of forecast combinations describes how combining forecasts can reduce the risk of picking the wrong single model, while stressing that member quality and diversity still matter. Two ways to combine the forecasts Each member returns quantile forecasts. The two main recipes use different rules to turn those forecasts into one predictive distribution and its median. Probabilistic Ensemble: the recommended default The Probabilistic Ensemble (uniform probability pooling) gives each member equal influence, pools their quantile forecasts in probability space, and extracts the requested quantiles from the combined values. Because the weights are fixed, there is no fitting step and no weighting hyperparameters to tune for a new series. The forecast combination puzzle offers useful motivation: in point forecasting, simple equal-weight combinations have often held up well against methods with estimated weights. This recipe applies the same equal-influence idea to probabilistic forecasts. It is the default loaded in the example above. IQR Ensemble: an adaptive alternative The IQR Ensemble weights members according to their forecast spread, giving narrower intervals greater influence. It approximates each member’s interquartile range from the closest available quantiles around the 25th and 75th percentiles. Weights vary by sample, target, and horizon step, and like the Probabilistic Ensemble, nothing is fitted from historical forecast errors. Isotonic regression keeps the combined quantiles from crossing. A narrower interval does not necessarily mean a more accurate or better-calibrated forecast, and IQR weighting can favor an overconfident member. If you want to experiment, the recipe exposes a temperature setting (higher values move the weights toward uniform) and an optional cap on any single member's weight. Load the evaluated IQR recipe by changing only the subfolder: ensemble = QuantileEnsembleForecaster.from_pretrained( "ibm-granite/granite-timeseries-ensemble-r1" , subfolder= "recipes/granite-iqr" , ) Which method should I use? Your goal Start with Why A simple default Probabilistic Ensemble Equal influence, no fitted weights Adaptive weighting based on forecast spread IQR Ensemble Influence varies with each member's predicted spread Start with the Probabilistic Ensemble. If forecast spread looks informative for your application, compare the IQR Ensemble against it on representative data, since accuracy and calibration depend on the series and the horizon. Does the ensemble improve on its members? We evaluated both recipes on 97 GIFT-Eval dataset configurations. The models forecast without fine-tuning, and test targets were not used to select or fit the aggregation method. Here we compare the official ensemble submission results with the four constituent models, using published leaderboard scores and ranks captured on 20 October 2026. GIFT-Eval reports MASE for point forecasts and CRPS/MWQL (the benchmark's mean_weighted_sum_quantile_loss metric) for probabilistic forecasts. Scores are normalized to Seasonal Naive and geometrically averaged across configurations. Lower is better. Forecast MASE ↓ MASE Rank ↓ CRPS / MWQL ↓ CRPS Rank ↓ Granite Ensemble R1 — Prob 0.683 ★ 47.175 ★ 0.471 50.948 Granite Ensemble R1 — IQR 0.684 48.773 0.471 47.619 ★ Granite PatchTST-FM-r2 0.685 51.371 0.467 ★ 48.918 Granite FlowState-r1.1 0.701 66.474 0.490 69.485 Granite PatchTST-FM-r1 0.717 74.794 0.488 68.134 Granite TTM-r3 0.724 83.062 0.520 88.959 ★ Best value among the forecasts shown. Lower is better. Rank columns average per-configuration ranks against the full GIFT-Eval reference leaderboard, not just these six forecasts, so rank values can shift as entries are added to the leaderboard. Both ensembles outperform all four individual members on aggregate MASE and average MASE Rank. The Probabilistic Ensemble achieves the lowest MASE among these six forecasts: 0.683 compared with 0.685 for PatchTST-FM-r2. Lower average MASE Rank indicates stronger relative point-forecast performance across GIFT-Eval’s diverse dataset configurations. Together, these results support the ensemble as a practical starting point, without requiring developers to select the strongest individual architecture in advance. The MASE margin over the best single member is small, so the main benefit is robustness: you get comparable or better aggregate accuracy without knowing in advance which architecture will suit your data. PatchTST-FM-r2 retains the lowest aggregate CRPS/MWQL score. The IQR Ensemble achieves the lowest average CRPS Rank among these six forecasts, while the Probabilistic Ensemble ranks behind PatchTST-FM-r2 on that measure. Aggregate error and average rank therefore favor different choices. In the 20 October 2026 comparison, the ensemble approach ranks 3rd among eligible systems on MASE Rank and CRPS Rank. The figure below shows both recipes alongside the ten best eligible reference systems per metric. Some systems, including entries excluded as fine-tuned or non-permissively licensed, score better than either recipe, so the value of the ensemble is not that it tops the leaderboard. It is that a single default delivers strong, consistent results across many series without requiring you to choose a member. Figure: GIFT-Eval average-rank standings on 20 October 2026, showing both Granite ensembles alongside the ten best eligible reference systems per metric. Eligible systems have replication code and no declared test-data leakage; fine-tuned entries and systems with known non-permissive licenses or member dependencies are excluded. Rank values are taken directly from the published overall leaderboard snapshot; filtering changes which systems are displayed, not their rank values. Extend the recipe to other forecasters The default recipe uses four Granite models, but the common Forecaster interface also accepts compatible external models. You can change the member mix or the aggregation method and keep the same downstream forecast format, with no merging or retraining of member checkpoints. That makes it easier to fit the ensemble into an existing forecasting stack, and to add forecasters suited to your domain as your needs evolve. The repository also includes expanded recipes that add IBM Research checkpoints. These carry separate license terms, including non-commercial and research-use restrictions, so review each member's model card before using them. For any new combination, check forecast compatibility, accuracy, calibration, latency, and licensing. Evaluate the recipe for your application GIFT-Eval is a broad benchmark, but aggregate gains don’t mean every series benefits, and average ranks don’t establish calibration. The way to find out how the recipes behave for your application is to backtest them on representative data: Match your use case . Use historical forecast windows that reflect the data available at each forecast origin, the horizon you need, and the series you expect to serve. Compare like with like . Run the Probabilistic Ensemble, the IQR Ensemble, and a strong individual member (such as PatchTST-FM-r2) on the same windows. Look beyond point error . Assess quantile loss alongside MASE, and check the empirical coverage of the 0.1 to 0.9 interval against its nominal 80%. Measure the cost . Record runtime and memory use to judge whether the benefit of combining four models justifies it for your workload. Keep two limitations in mind. The current recipe forecasts multivariate channels independently, without using cross-channel information, and it loads four member checkpoints, which increases inference time and memory relative to a single member. Member context limits, horizons, preprocessing, and missing-value handling also differ, and neither aggregation method guarantees calibration or robustness under distribution shift, so keep monitoring forecasts after deployment. Try it on your data The recommended starting point is the default four-model recipe: Granite Timeseries Ensemble on Hugging Face Getting-started notebook Granite TSFM repository GIFT-Eval benchmark Load the default recipe to get median and quantile forecasts from all four Granite architectures in one call, and adapt the recipe as your needs evolve. References ECMWF: Ensemble weather forecasting NOAA: North American Multi-Model Ensemble FlowState: Sampling-Rate-Equivariant Time-Series Forecasting Tiny Time Mixers (TTMs): Fast Pre-trained Models for Enhanced Zero/Few-Shot Forecasting of Multivariate Time Series Revisiting the Generic Transformer: Deconstructing a Strong Baseline for Time Series Foundation Models Forecast combinations: an over 50-year review Smith and Wallis (2009), A Simple Explanation of the Forecast Combination Puzzle Models mentioned in this article 5 Spaces mentioned in this article 1 More from this author ALTK-Evolve: How learned memory tops the τ²-bench leaderboard on customer service tasks without a frontier model 27 October 20, 2026 Your Agent Aced the Task.
