items.title: NVIDIA Kumo Relational Outperforms Supervised Machine Learning on Relational Data, No Training Required
items.content:
Back to Articles a]:hidden"> NVIDIA Kumo Relational Outperforms Supervised Machine Learning on Relational Data, No Training Required Enterprise + Article Published October 21, 2026 Upvote 32 +26 Joshua Przybylko jprzybylko Follow nvidia Valter Hudovernik valterh-nv Follow nvidia Federico Lopez flopeznv Follow nvidia Akihiro Nitta akihironitta-nv Follow nvidia Ramona Bendias RBendiasN Follow nvidia Ardrian Wong aw777 Follow nvidia Jure Leskovec profjure Follow nvidia Matthias Fey rusty1s Follow nvidia :last-child]:mb-0"> TL;DR NVIDIA Kumo Relational is a pre-trained relational foundation model that makes predictions directly on enterprise databases. Given a predictive query, it gathers historical examples as context examples and predicts outcomes such as churn, demand, or fraud in a single forward pass. It needs no task-specific training, no feature engineering, and no flattening of tables. Kumo Relational is the first few-shot foundation model to outperform supervised machine learning on common relational benchmarks. Across 41 tasks on 15 databases, it beats supervised relational deep learning models and expert-engineered gradient-boosted tree pipelines, and on the SAP SALT enterprise benchmark it surpasses AutoGluon ensembles by 8% in mean reciprocal rank (MRR). It scales to databases with 500B+ rows and works for humans and agents alike, through NVIDIA's open-source, GPU-native structured-data-models and kumo-engine libraries, or as an NVIDIA NIM. Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.12596 Model Code: https://github.com/NVIDIA/structured-data-models Model Weights: https://huggingface.co/nvidia/Kumo-Relational Client Code: https://github.com/NVIDIA/structured-data-models-client NIM Documentation: https://docs.nvidia.com/sdgm/rfm/overview The Shift to Structured Data Foundation Models Foundation models have already rewritten the playbook for language and vision. Not long ago, production NLP meant a dedicated model per task, each fed by its own pipeline of tokenization, lemmatization, and n-grams. LLMs made that stack largely obsolete for three reasons: they were more accurate than the best task-specific models, far simpler to put into production, and flexible enough to open a new era of agentic applications. The same shift is now underway for structured data. Relational databases power the world's most critical business decisions, yet predictive modeling on them still requires weeks of feature engineering, task-specific training, and tuned pipelines. Structured data foundation models change that for the same three reasons: Better accuracy today: As drop-in replacements, these models already beat many production pipelines, especially XGBoost. On RelBench V1 classification tasks, Kumo Relational outperforms gradient-boosted trees on expert-engineered features by nearly 4 AUROC points on average. On SAP SALT, it beats XGBoost on engineered features by 7 MRR points out of the box and by 13 MRR points after fine-tuning. These results make a compelling case for replacing production XGBoost pipelines with Kumo Relational. Simplicity and agility: One pre-trained model replaces separate pipelines for individual tasks. A new prediction becomes a query instead of a project, so ML teams can finally take on use cases that traditional ML made too laborious to build at every level of the organization. Agents that can predict: LLMs let agents read, write, and reason. Structured data foundation models let them anticipate what happens next, such as which customer will churn, and act on it. Kumo Relational is already built to be called by agents, and its Predictive Query Language (PQL) gives them a simple interface for asking predictive questions. Today, we are introducing Kumo Relational ( Paper , GitHub , HuggingFace ), a pre-trained foundation model that brings this paradigm to relational data. Connect a database, describe what to predict, and get predictions in a single forward pass. No training required. How Kumo Relational Works Most foundation models for structured data operate on a single flat table. Real-world data lives in relational databases instead: users connected to orders connected to products, all evolving over time. Flattening these relationships into one row through manual aggregation ( e.g. , "average order value in the last 30 days") loses fine-grained structural signals and takes significant human effort. Kumo Relational is a Relational Foundation Model that operates directly on the database, respecting its tables, foreign keys, and timestamps. It is pre-trained once on synthetic relational data that reflects real-world datasets and adapts to each new task through in-context learning by reasoning over context examples at inference time. Each example pairs a local subgraph around an entity at a point in time with its ground-truth target ( e.g. , "this user churned" or "this item sold 142 units"). Figure 1. Overview of the Kumo Relational system. Connect a database, specify a predictive query, and Kumo Relational handles the rest, from context generation to model inference. To make a prediction, Kumo Relational has to do three things: (1) understand the values within each table, (2) relate records across tables, and (3) relate context examples with known targets to the entity being predicted. Here is how it works: Figure 2. Kumo Relational architecture: (a) context input, (b) reasoning within tables, (c) reasoning across tables. Automatic Context Generation: Tasks are written in the Predictive Query Language (PQL) , a declarative interface where you state what to predict rather than how. For temporal tasks, Kumo Relational replays historical database states: it samples entity-centric subgraphs up to an anchor timestamp and computes each target from events after that timestamp, while serving the model only the data from before it. This prevents data leakage. Reasoning Within Tables: A lightweight network processes each table independently via column attention (relating values within a column) and row attention (relating features within a row). The model learns which columns and rows matter for the current prediction and filters out noise before it propagates. Reasoning Across Tables: A larger network distributes the row embeddings across the relational structure via graph attention over primary-key/foreign-key relationships, followed by cross-sample attention across context examples. This is where relational reasoning happens, such as linking a user's profile to their transaction history. Because this stage works on row embeddings rather than on every cell in every table, the design avoids quadratic cost and scales to large contexts and deeper subgraphs. How Kumo Relational Was Built Kumo Relational is pre-trained on entirely synthetic relational data simulated to reflect real-world relational databases with diverse predictive queries. Pre-training proceeds in stages, from single tables to increasingly complex relational structures. The diverse relational databases needed for pre-training are rarely public, so synthetic data fills the gap. Kumo Relational's generator builds on the approach of PluRel (Kothapalli et al., ICML 2026), which extends single-table data generators to full relational databases. PluRel generates each database in three stages: a schema, foreign-key links between rows that cluster as they do in real data, and column values from Structural Causal Models with temporal trends and cross-table dependencies. Generation is lightweight, so pre-training data is effectively unlimited. Pre-training loss follows a power law as synthetic databases are added, with gains that carry over to real databases. Through this pre-training, the model learns to filter, correlate, and aggregate information across tables instead of relying on fixed aggregations. Performance In the paper, we evaluated Kumo Relational on 41 benchmarks across 15 relational databases from RelBench V1 and V2, SAP SALT, and 4DBInfer, spanning e-commerce, medical, enterprise, social, and academic domains. None of these datasets were seen in pre-training. Kumo Relational outperforms the strongest supervised models in both classification and regression, including relational deep learning models and expert-engineered tabular ensembles. It is the top-performing in-context learning model on the RelBench leaderboard . On RelArena-α , it sits on the accuracy-efficiency Pareto front: Figure 3. RelArena-α leaderboard as of 2026-09-21: Elo across tasks versus total task runtime (log scale). Kumo Relational is about 430× faster than rtl-plurel at similar accuracy. On the SAP SALT enterprise benchmark, Kumo Relational surpasses large AutoGluon ensembles by 8% in mean reciprocal rank (MRR), and fine-tuning extends its lead over AutoGluon to 16%. It also holds up under hard conditions: it performs well with as little as 0.2% of the training data as context, stays stable when up to 75% of foreign-key links are removed, and barely degrades when noisy columns are added. Limitations Kumo Relational performs best on data with meaningful relationships and temporal dynamics, such as user behavior over time. On tasks with very large training sets, task-specific supervised models may still edge out in-context predictions. Predictive signals must be reachable within a limited number of hops. Demo Kumo Relational runs in-context learning natively over databases: in memory , through database and warehouse connectors , or through kumo-engine that handles 500B+ rows via memory-mapped I/O at up to 5 GB/s. The model itself is available in NVIDIA's newly released, GPU-native structured-data-models library, the same open-source library that powers our sister model, Kumo Tabular . The library downloads the weights from the Hugging Face Hub on first use, so you can load the model in a GPU-backed notebook and predict directly from it. The interface is designed to naturally extend tabular foundation models to relational signal by passing additional related multi-table context and query information: import sdm # pip install structured-data-models model = sdm.models.KumoRelational(device= "cuda" ) pred = model( # In-context training table (fkeys/timestamps/targets): x_context=sdm.TableTensor(...), y_context=sdm.TableTensor(...), # Prediction examples (fkeys/timestamps): x_query=sdm.TableTensor(...), # Multi-table information for context/prediction entities: related_context_tables=sdm.RelatedTables(tables={...}), related_query_tables=sdm.RelatedTables(tables={...}), ) See the library's relational examples for RelBench and SAP SALT pipelines. To run the model as a separate service instead, deploy it as an NVIDIA NIM and point the open-source structured-data-models-client at it from your notebook. You write the prediction in PQL, and the client gathers the context examples and related tables, then sends the request: import sdm_client # pip install 'structured-data-models-client[relational]' client = sdm_client.SDMClient(url= "http://localhost:8001" ) # NIM URL query = sdm_client.PredictiveQuery( # Prediction task in Predictive Query Language (PQL): "PREDICT COUNT(orders.*, 0, 30, days) FOR EACH users.user_id" , # Multi-table data as pandas DataFrames (keys/links inferred): { "users" : ..., "orders" : ...}, ) pred = client.predict( # Context examples and related tables for the entities to predict: query.materialize(indices=[ 1 , 2 , 3 ]), model=sdm_client.KumoRelational(), ) See the client's example notebooks for end-to-end runs against a local NIM and on Databricks. Start Building with NVIDIA Kumo Relational NVIDIA Kumo Relational is available today. Read the research paper , explore the quickstart notebook , or start making predictions on your own data. The code is released under the Apache 2.0 license and the model weights under the OpenMDW License Agreement, version 1.1. NVIDIA believes Trustworthy AI is a shared responsibility, and we have established policies and practices to enable development for a wide array of AI applications. When downloaded or used in accordance with our terms of service, developers should work with their supporting model team to ensure this model meets requirements for the relevant industry and use case and addresses unforeseen product misuse. Please report model quality, risk, security vulnerabilities, or NVIDIA AI concerns here . items.title: Granite Speech 5.0: Transcribe, Translate, and Attribute more Accurately and Faster
items.content: Back to Articles a]:hidden"> Granite Speech 5.0: Transcribe, Translate, and Attribute more Accurately and Faster Enterprise Article Published October 21, 2026 Upvote 26 +20 George Saon gsaon Follow ibm-granite Brian Kingsbury bedkingsbury Follow ibm-granite Ron Hoory rhoory Follow ibm-granite Vishal Sunder vishalsunder Follow ibm-granite Zvi Kons konszvi Follow ibm-granite Jeff Kuo ibm-jeffkuo Follow ibm-granite Samuel Thomas sthomas12 Follow ibm-granite Avihu Dekel Avihu Follow ibm-granite Hagai Aronowitz hagaia Follow ibm-granite Takashi Fukuda fukuda1 Follow ibm-granite Tohru Nagano tohru3 Follow ibm-granite Sashi Novitasari sasnov Follow ibm-granite Masayuki Suzuki szuk Follow ibm-granite Madison Lee kristunlee Follow ibm-granite :last-child]:mb-0"> We're excited to share three updates to IBM's Granite Speech collection: a new speech-language model, granite-speech-5.0-2b , and revised versions of two models the community already uses, granite-speech-5.0-470m-turboctc and granite-speech-4.1-2b-plus . Together they cover the full range of enterprise speech work: transcription and translation with high accuracy, extremely fast transcription at the edge, and recordings where who spoke, and when, matter as much as what was said. Model Status What's new Best for granite-speech-5.0-2b New More accurate, noise- and reverb-robust automatic speech recognition (ASR), language-ID prompting, 2,000-term keyword biasing, better long-form translation High-accuracy multilingual transcription and translation granite-speech-5.0-470m-turboctc Updated Multilingual, native punctuation and capitalization, and more robust to noise and reverb High-throughput and on-device transcription granite-speech-4.1-2b-plus Updated Improved speaker attribution, timestamps, keyword biasing, and long-speech performance Meetings, calls, and other multi-speaker recordings Granite Speech 5.0 2B: more accurate, more robust, more control granite-speech-5.0-2b is the successor to granite-speech-4.1-2b at the same parameter count. It transcribes English, French, German, Spanish, Portuguese, and Japanese, and translates to and from English in those languages, plus English to Italian and Mandarin. It was trained on 390,000 hours of public audio, plus synthetic data built for Japanese ASR, keyword biasing, and translation. What's new compared with 4.1 2B Speech: More accurate, more robust English ASR: Higher accuracy on English short-form benchmarks, and better handling of noise, reverberation, and distant-microphone speech. Language ID prompting: Name the input language in the prompt to steer multilingual transcription. Better long-form and conversational translation: Translation holds up for longer with more natural speech, not just short read sentences. Keyword lists up to 2,000 terms: Bias transcription and translation toward product names, people, and acronyms, in every supported language. Punctuation and capitalization on request: Ask for formatted output in the prompt; capitalization F1 ranges from 89.7 to 99.5 across our test sets. The model ships under Apache 2.0 with support in Transformers, vLLM, llama.cpp, and mlx-audio for Apple Silicon. Chart 1: granite-speech-5.0-2b ranks #2 among top open-weight ASR models on average English WER (5.06%). Lower is better. Results are official, as of 21 October 2026, and averaged over the Open ASR Leaderboard’s public English short-form test sets. Granite Speech 5.0 Turbo CTC: now multilingual, more robust, and even faster When we introduced Turbo CTC in August , it was an English-only, 470M-parameter encoder built for speed. This revision keeps that footprint and adds the three things users asked for most: Multilingual transcription: English, Japanese, Spanish, German, French, Italian, and Portuguese. Native punctuation and capitalization: Transcripts come out ready to read, with no separate punctuation or truecasing step. More robust in difficult acoustics: Training that explicitly targets reverberant audio makes Turbo CTC more robust in echoey rooms and far-field recordings. It's also faster. By compiling a single Conformer block and reusing its graph across the stack, we cut warmup time and pushed Turbo CTC to 19,870 RTFx on the Open ASR Leaderboard, up from roughly 12,600 RTFx at launch: about 1.6x faster, at the same accuracy level. Chart 2: Average WER vs. RTFx on the Open ASR Leaderboard (English short-form, 9 public test sets, as of October 2026). Lower WER and higher RTFx are better; RTFx is on a log scale. Granite Speech 4.1 2B Plus: better at who said what, and when The updated granite-speech-4.1-2b-plus is tuned for the recordings enterprises actually have: meetings, support calls, and interviews with several speakers running long. It keeps the 4.1 name because the architecture, prompt format, and API are unchanged, so it's a drop-in replacement for the current model with improved weights. This revision improves four areas: Speaker attribution: More accurate labeling of who is speaking. Word diarization error rate (WDER) drops 7%, and speaker-attributed WER (cpWER) drops 7% overall. Timestamps: Average timestamp shift (AAS) is cut by more than half, yielding tighter timing in captions, search, and review. Long-speech performance: WER on long-form test sets drops 24%. Keyword biasing: Errors on biased keywords fall 45% with 20-term keyword lists. Capability Metric Previous release Updated model Timestamps, all speech AAS (average timestamp shift) 210.86 98.54 Timestamps, short speech AAS (average timestamp shift) 29.27 26.20 Keyword biasing Biased-word WER, 20-term lists 11.79 6.48 Long-form speech WER, long-form test sets 13.53 10.22 Speaker attribution WDER 4.40 4.10 Speaker-attributed transcripts cpWER 30.50 28.48 Table 1: All metrics are error rates, so lower is better. For more detailed results, see the model card . Get started Not sure which model to pick? Start here: Need high transcription accuracy, translation, or keyword biasing? Use granite-speech-5.0-2b . Need raw speed or on-device transcription? Use granite-speech-5.0-470m-turboctc , and try it in the browser with our WebGPU streaming demo . Working with meetings or multi-speaker calls? Use granite-speech-4.1-2b-plus . These models are all released under an Apache 2.0 license with native support in Transformers. Full evaluation results, architecture details, training data, and usage examples are on each model card. We recommend pairing them with Granite Guardian for production deployments that need additional risk detection. Give them a try and let us know what you think! items.title: TorchNeuron: running HF models on AWS Trainium is easier than ever
items.content:
Back to Articles a]:hidden"> TorchNeuron: running HF models on AWS Trainium is easier than ever Published October 19, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 32 +26 Régis Pierrard regisss Follow Simon Pagezy pagezyhf Follow Michael Benayoun michaelbenayoun Follow Jingya Huang Jingya Follow Alvaro Moran tengomucho Follow David Corvoysier dacorvo Follow Jeff Boudier jeffboudier Follow :last-child]:mb-0"> TorchNeuron provides a new native backend for PyTorch on AWS Trainium. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels natively support it, making it easier than ever to run models on Trainium and to share them on the HF hub. TorchNeuron TorchNeuron is a PyTorch plugin that brings a new backend for Trainium enabling support for eager mode, torch.compile and native distributed APIs like FSDP and TP. Read the Pytorch blog to learn more about TorchNeuron. Starting Oct. 20, 2026, TorchNeuron will be available as a public beta. Researchers and developers will be able to install it with pip install torch-neuronx . New backend, native interface in HF libraries To date, the Hugging Face experience on AWS Trainium and Inferentia — AI chips designed respectively for cost-effective training and inference at scale — has been delivered through optimum-neuron . This library relies on the torch-neuronx package, which is based on PyTorch XLA. It was the natural choice at the time, but it meant thinking like a compiler: lazy tensors instead of eager execution, static shapes only, a recompilation for every graph break. Optimum Neuron existed to hide that complexity, and maintained custom code (modeling classes, trainers, etc) to do so. TorchNeuron changes this. It integrates directly into PyTorch and exposes neuron as a native device, with eager execution, PyTorch's own distributed primitives (DTensor, FSDP2) and torch.compile . For the Hugging Face libraries, Trainium becomes a device like any other: Transformers, Diffusers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL run on it directly, with the same classes and scripts you would use on any other accelerator. From now on, we recommend that Neuron users use these libraries directly instead of going through Optimum Neuron. Transformers Inference Text generation is now natively supported in Transformers for a wide range of models. With TorchNeuron, 89% of the top 100 most-used text-generation model architectures are supported out of the box, compared to 46% with Optimum Neuron v0.4.5. You just need to pass the device_map=neuron argument in your code and your model will be moved to the Neuron devices. The following is an example of text-generation with tensor parallelism, which will enable to fully benefit from your Neuron instance. Note that it uses a static cache for generation as this is strongly recommended with Neuron to prevent frequent recompilations. import os import torch import torch.distributed as dist import torch_neuronx # noqa: F401 from torch.distributed import DeviceMesh from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer, GenerationConfig from transformers.distributed import DistributedConfig from transformers.generation.configuration_utils import CompileConfig MODEL_ID = "Qwen/Qwen3.8-27B" MAX_SEQ_LEN = 1024 PREFILL_CHUNK_SIZE = 512 dist.init_process_group(backend= "neuron" ) world_size = dist.get_world_size() model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained( MODEL_ID, dtype=torch.bfloat16, distributed_config=DistributedConfig(tp_size=world_size), device_mesh=DeviceMesh( "neuron" , list ( range (world_size))), ). eval () tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(MODEL_ID) if tokenizer.pad_token is None : tokenizer.pad_token = tokenizer.eos_token tokenizer.padding_side = "left" inputs = tokenizer.apply_chat_template( [{ "role" : "user" , "content" : "The future of AI is" }], add_generation_prompt= True , padding= True , tokenizer_kwargs={ "pad_to_multiple_of" : PREFILL_CHUNK_SIZE}, return_tensors= "pt" , ) generation_config = GenerationConfig( max_new_tokens= 128 , do_sample= False , use_cache= True , pad_token_id=tokenizer.pad_token_id, eos_token_id=tokenizer.eos_token_id, cache_implementation= "static" , max_cache_len=MAX_SEQ_LEN, prefill_chunk_size=PREFILL_CHUNK_SIZE, compile_config=CompileConfig(backend= "neuron" , fullgraph= False , dynamic= False ), ) with torch.no_grad(): output_ids = model.generate( inputs[ "input_ids" ], attention_mask=inputs[ "attention_mask" ], generation_config=generation_config, ) if dist.get_rank() == 0 : prompt_len = inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[ 1 ] print (tokenizer.decode(output_ids[ 0 , prompt_len:], skip_special_tokens= True )) Training Now that Neuron is a native PyTorch device, training on Trainium uses the same Hugging Face libraries as any other accelerator: Transformers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL. You no longer need a dedicated trainer or a Neuron-specific fork of the model code. A standard TRL fine-tuning script runs on a Trainium instance with only a few Neuron-specific settings. Here is a supervised fine-tuning script built on TRL's SFTTrainer . If you have fine-tuned a model with TRL on GPUs before, it should look familiar. import os import torch from datasets import load_dataset from transformers.distributed import DistributedConfig from trl import ModelConfig, ScriptArguments, SFTConfig, SFTTrainer, TrlParser def main ( script_args, training_args, model_args ): # The Neuron backend can't compile Dynamo's automatic dynamic shapes yet (https://github.com/huggingface/trl/issues/7660) torch._dynamo.config.automatic_dynamic_shapes = False training_args.model_init_kwargs = { "revision" : model_args.model_revision, "trust_remote_code" : training_args.trust_remote_code, "attn_implementation" : model_args.attn_implementation, "dtype" : model_args.dtype, "device_map" : None , } if int (os.environ.get( "WORLD_SIZE" , "1" )) > 1 : # The model is sharded on the TP x FSDP grid as its weights are loaded training_args.model_init_kwargs[ "distributed_config" ] = DistributedConfig( tp_size= int (os.environ.get( "TP_SIZE" , "1" )), fsdp_size= int (os.environ.get( "FSDP_SIZE" , "1" )), ) # Prepare dataset train_dataset = load_dataset( script_args.dataset_name, name=script_args.dataset_config, split=script_args.dataset_train_split, ) # UltraChat also has a string `prompt` column, which makes TRL treat it as a prompt-completion dataset. train_dataset = train_dataset.select_columns([ "messages" ]) # Training trainer = SFTTrainer( model=model_args.model_name_or_path, args=training_args, train_dataset=train_dataset, ) trainer.train() trainer.save_model(training_args.output_dir) trainer.end() if __name__ == "__main__" : parser = TrlParser((ScriptArguments, SFTConfig, ModelConfig)) script_args, training_args, model_args = parser.parse_args_and_config() main(script_args, training_args, model_args) Parallelism is handled natively by Transformers. You put a DistributedConfig with the tensor-parallel (TP) and FSDP sizes in model_init_kwargs , SFTTrainer passes it to from_pretrained , and the model is sharded as its weights are loaded. The Trainer sees that the model is already distributed and does not wrap it again. You don't need an --fsdp flag or an Accelerate FSDP config. Nothing in the script is tied to Trainium: the same code runs on any hardware. A few things are worth knowing when you run it on Trainium: Static shapes. The script disables automatic dynamic shapes in torch.compile and uses wrapped packing to produce sequences of up to 2048 tokens. With TRL ≥ 1.16, batches on Neuron are padded to a multiple of 128 tokens, limiting the number of input shapes. Compiled graphs are reused for subsequent steps with the same shapes. torch.compile on. Passing --torch_compile true is all it takes: on a Trainium instance, torch.compile detects the device and picks the Neuron backend automatically, with nothing else to configure. Async weight loading off. The built-in asynchronous weight loading in Transformers is not supported on Neuron, so for now we disable it with HF_DEACTIVATE_ASYNC_LOAD=1 . The command below launches training with torchrun , which starts one process per NeuronCore. TP_SIZE and FSDP_SIZE set the parallelism layout, and their product is the number of processes: here 4 x 8 = 32, matching --nproc_per_node . The 32 processes form a 4 x 8 grid. Tensor parallelism splits each layer across the 4 cores of a TP group, and FSDP shards the parameters, gradients and optimizer state across the 8 TP groups. TP_SIZE=4 FSDP_SIZE=8 HF_DEACTIVATE_ASYNC_LOAD=1 uv run torchrun --nproc_per_node=32 sft_neuron_example.py \ --model_name_or_path Qwen/Qwen3-8B \ --dataset_name HuggingFaceH4/ultrachat_200k \ --dataset_train_split train_sft \ --output_dir Qwen3-8B-sft-tp4-fsdp8 \ --dtype bfloat16 \ --max_length 2048 \ --packing true \ --packing_strategy wrapped \ --learning_rate 2e-5 \ --warmup_steps 0.03 \ --num_train_epochs 1 \ --logging_steps 2 \ --per_device_train_batch_size 4 \ --gradient_accumulation_steps 4 \ --save_only_model true \ --torch_compile true We ran it on 8 Trainium2 chips (32 NeuronCores), which is half a trn2.48xlarge instance. Training runs to completion, and trainer.save_model writes a standard Transformers checkpoint. Nothing in it is tied to Neuron: you can push it to the Hugging Face Hub as is and load it on any other hardware. Diffusers Inference Many pipelines from the Diffusers library are compatible with TorchNeuron in eager and compiled mode. FLUX.1-dev, FLUX.2, Qwen-Image, Qwen-Image-2.1 and H3 are also compatible with tensor parallelism to make the most of your Neuron devices. The following is an example showing how you can use TP: import torch, torch.distributed as dist, torch_neuronx # TP from torch.distributed.device_mesh import DeviceMesh # TP from diffusers import QwenImage21Pipeline, QwenImage21Transformer2DModel, TensorParallelConfig # Distributed devices initialization dist.init_process_group(backend= "neuron" ) # TP dev = torch.neuron.current_device() mesh = DeviceMesh( "neuron" , list ( range ( 8 ))) # TP=8 # Pipeline initialization model = "Qwen/Qwen-Image-2.1" transformer = QwenImage21Transformer2DModel.from_pretrained( model, subfolder= "transformer" , torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16, parallel_config=TensorParallelConfig(mesh=mesh), # TP ) pipe = QwenImage21Pipeline.from_pretrained( model, transformer=transformer, torch_dtype=torch.bfloat16, ) pipe.vae.to(dev) pipe.transformer.compile_repeated_blocks(backend= "neuron" , fullgraph= True , dynamic= False ) # Image generation emb, mask, _ = pipe.encode_prompt(prompt= "A capybara wearing a wizard hat, oil painting" , device= "cpu" ) # text encoder stays on CPU image = pipe( prompt_embeds=emb.to(dev), prompt_embeds_mask=mask.to(dev) if mask is not None else None , height= 1024 , width= 1024 , num_inference_steps= 40 , generator=torch.Generator( "cpu" ).manual_seed( 0 ), # same noise on every rank ).images[ 0 ] if dist.get_rank() == 0 : image.save( "out.png" ) You can run this piece of code with: NEURON_LOGICAL_NC_CONFIG=2 torchrun --nproc_per_node=8 run.py . More and more pipleines will be compatible with TP. If a pipeline you like is not, you can also add support for it following this guide . Kernels Make sure to check out the kernels from the Neuron team as more and more Neuron kernels will become available on the Hub to speed up your models. Neuron kernels can be written using the Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI), which gives lower control to optimize operations. This way, users can run their own custom operations and share them on the hub. You can use for example this kernel to speed up your vision transformers with up to a x2.4 speedup on Trainium! Acknowledgments Special thanks to the AWS team for their work on TorchNeuron and for their reactivity to our feedback to make the HF integration as good as possible. items.title: Grounding AI agents in biological reality: Building blocks for autonomous wet labs
items.description: General Science
items.content: Grounding AI agents in biological reality: Building blocks for autonomous wet labs October 16, 2026 Pooja Rao, Research Scientist, Petar Sirkovic, Software Engineer, and Annalisa Pawlosky, Research Scientist, Google We are bringing AI agents to the wet-lab bench at Google Research to navigate complex biological landscapes. By grounding agents in physical lab robotics, we can run fast closed-loop molecular design cycles where agents learn how to learn, ultimately discovering single-digit nanomolar protein binders for cancer targets. Quick links VERID paper Agentic aptamer sandbox paper Epitope excision paper Share Frontier AI systems have the potential to transform biology research and drug discovery by intelligently navigating vast combinatorial search spaces (e.g., a single 100-amino-acid protein spans at least 20 100 possible sequences) calling for dynamic multi-candidate exploration. Our long-term research vision is that AI agents will not only ideate and analyze, but also run lab experiments to test their hypotheses, learn from the results, and self-improve to solve complex problems — all driven by human scientific agency. Realizing this vision requires solving two intertwined challenges: First, frontier models still do not reason reliably about 3-dimensional geometry and physical state — which poses a problem in the automation of the specialized liquid-handling robots that move reagents, track volumes, and execute molecular biology protocols in a wet lab. Second, while agentic hypothesis generation and in-silico design are advancing rapidly, needing repeated cycles of real-world feedback to validate the proposals and navigate vast search spaces, real-world wet-lab experiments have not kept pace, making experimental readouts more of a bottleneck than ever. In this post we share three research projects highlighting our progress on bridging the gap between in-silico AI exploration and real-world wet-lab experimentation: Enabling AI agents to perform safe, resource efficient experimentation grounded in physical measurements by using the VERID framework. Demonstrating closed-loop agentic scientific discoveries on our prototypes for aptamer and de-novo protein design. Grounding agents in physical reality First, we present the VERified Infrastructure for Discovery Laboratories (VERID) framework to bridge the gap between the high-level reasoning of AI agents and the complex, error-prone physical reality of a wet lab. It is a semantic digital twin of the laboratory workcell, i.e., a live, stateful 3D volumetric entity tree that tracks everything from robotic arm geometry to individual well volumes, reagent identities, and pipette tip inventory. The safety of a command depends on the live physical context as well as the code. An agent can generate syntactically valid code that is physically impossible (e.g., lowering an 8-channel pipette into a narrow trough that is too short), logistically invalid (e.g., aspirating from a depleted well), or scientifically compromised by unmodeled fluidic effects. play looping video pause looping video unmute video mute video Through VERID, an AI agent plans, simulates, and executes liquid-handling protocols on a liquid handling robot, combining synchronized multi-camera views with live state tracking to refine experiments across cycles. Built on top of the open-source PyLabRobot framework , VERID provides four core capabilities: Live 3D state tracking: Allow agents to check deck layout, well volumes, and available tips before acting. Fast virtual dry runs: Simulate protocols in seconds to catch collisions or empty wells before touching reagents. Hardware safety checks: Block invalid commands before they reach the robot. Synchronized video and action logs: Capture a complete record of every run for research rigor, reproducibility, and debugging. In our report , we show these capabilities in action through case studies. First, synchronized video and execution traces caught uneven dye stratification caused by dispensing too close to the well floor, allowing the agent to refine its mixing strategy. In the same campaign, the persistent digital twin state allowed the agent to recover mid-run from a plate-reader failure without re-pipetting. Second, when the simulator rejected an 8-channel aspiration that physically wouldn't fit in a narrow trough, the agent replanned on the fly and designed a targeted factorial diagnostic isolating a subtle bias caused by residual tip-wall carryover that replication alone would have missed. Finally, in a closed-loop self-play campaign, an agent iteratively designed and ran robot experiments to reconstruct blinded dye mixtures from overhead camera images, identifying its own optical and fluidic artifacts across runs to improve accuracy more than fivefold. Reproducible execution and full trace logs — capturing procedural variables like dwell times, evaporation, and plate layout — lay the groundwork for agents to eventually be able to separate biological signals from experimental noise as they explore and refine many candidates in parallel across rounds. Learning to learn with aptamers Agents need real experimental readouts to refine their hypotheses as computational models do not capture the full picture of what happens in a wet-lab reaction and cannot replace empirical validation. In “ Aptamers as a sandbox for lab-in-the-loop agentic molecular discovery ”, we use protein-binding DNA aptamers to prototype the lab in a closed loop with AI agents over 3 design-test-iteration cycles. Aptamer discovery is a type of experiment common in research efforts for clinical biomarker discovery. A complete aptamer design-test-analyze cycle takes just 7–10 days, as DNA can be chemically synthesized in pooled libraries and read out directly by sequencing. In each round, agents design candidate sequences, which are screened against target proteins on magnetic beads to isolate functional binders, and then sequenced to return rich quantitative data for the next cycle. Agents iteratively design, synthesize, select, and sequence aptamers in a closed loop. Across three rounds on two protein targets with varying difficulty levels ( myoglobin and α-thrombin ), AI-driven rational and de novo design raised confirmed on-target hit rates as can be seen in the image below (to 33.5% and 42.1% for myoglobin and α-thrombin, respectively), though each target required identifying and overcoming a different wet-lab failure mode. On α-thrombin, Round 1 yielded 0% binders because fixed primer overhangs disrupted folding in 48% of sequences; once the agents introduced clamped flanking stems in Round 2 and diversified in Round 3, hit rates climbed to 26.0% and then 42.1% at 98.5% specificity. On myoglobin, as agents prioritized raw binding affinity in Round 2, they heavily enriched G-quadruplex motifs (63% of designs). While raw pull-down increased, the wet-lab data showed that most of these G-quadruplexes were non-specific "sticky" binders adhering to off-target proteins and bare magnetic beads, causing both target specificity (from 75.0% to 19.1%) and true, bead-corrected hit rate (from 10.2% to 3.7%) to plunge. Recognizing this artifact from the Round 2 readout, the agents autonomously revised their design rules for Round 3, capping promiscuous motifs, subtracting bead binders, and pivoting to non-G4 structural scaffolds to recover specificity (72.4%) and surge ninefold in on-target hit rate (33.5%). Across three rounds, agents learn from wet-lab readouts to recover target specificity and improve confirmed de novo hit rates on myoglobin ( left ) and α-thrombin ( right ). In the paper, we also examine how agents reason like scientists, analyzing data and suggesting tweaks to wet-lab protocols, but also sometimes think atypically, exploring sequence spaces that structural biologists might not. Accelerating de novo protein binder design Closing the loop for proteins is more complex. Unlike aptamers, which are chemically synthesized, proteins must be expressed biologically, so each loop adds cellular or cell-free selection, expression, and folding steps. Together with a larger sequence space, this creates bottlenecks on both the computational and wet-lab sides. In “ Agent-guided epitope excision enables economical de novo binder design ”, we applied our workflow to fibroblast activation protein alpha (FAP) , a large, challenging receptor overexpressed in solid tumors. In just a few experimental runs, the top designs yielded binders with single-digit nanomolar affinity, a level of tight, drug-like binding typically achieved only after extensive rounds of laboratory optimization. Surgical epitope excision accelerates structure prediction 8.6x ( left ), enabling a human–agent hybrid pipeline to nearly double the in-silico hit rate ( top right ) and discover single-digit nanomolar FAP binders in the wet lab ( bottom right ). Computationally, de novo binder design requires generating candidate backbones, designing sequences to fit them, and re-folding the resulting complexes to predict binding. That final re-folding step consumes the vast majority of GPU compute, as it scales quadratically with target length. By surgically excising just the local binding pocket during folding, our pipeline accelerated each cycle more than eightfold without losing structural accuracy. This turns decisions about where to bind and how much surrounding structure to include into tactical levers that LLM agents are well-suited to optimize. In a head-to-head comparison at equal compute, human–agent collaboration, where a scientist sets the high-level strategy and an agent drives tactical execution, nearly doubled the in-silico hit rate of a scientist working alone while uncovering hits across a much broader range of target sites. To scale wet-lab screening alongside our computational pipeline, we operationalized yeast surface display with fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS), a workflow that allows us to screen large libraries of engineered protein variants in parallel by fluorescence. Our next step is to weave these threads together, combining VERID’s fully traceable automation with closed-loop learning for protein discovery to enable agents to directly navigate complex, rugged biological search spaces in the wet lab. Safety In line with Google’s Frontier Safety Framework and our approach to bioresilience , we build safeguards across both the computational and wet-lab sides of our workflows: Safe testbeds and screening: We deliberately selected well-controlled, non-infectious biological systems without gain-of-function risk, as testbeds to evaluate agent behavior and catch drift early. Every designed sequence goes through biosecurity screening. Simulation before execution: Through VERID, agents never send unverified code directly to the liquid handling robots. Every protocol is dry-run in simulation and validated against the digital twin before touching reagents. Human oversight: Humans directly authorize and review designed sequences, verify wet-lab protocols, and supervise robot runs. As AI agents take on more of the design-test cycle, new safety and reliability challenges emerge. Moving toward an autonomous wet lab requires solving these open problems with opportunities for human agency and oversight: ensuring agents optimize for true target binding rather than unintended experimental shortcuts, verifying multi-step wet-lab protocols, and continuously monitoring agent reasoning and execution traces. From grounding agents in physical lab robotics, to running fast closed-loop aptamer cycles where agents learn to explore sequence space, to discovering single-digit nanomolar protein binders, these efforts form the building blocks for human-directed autonomous discovery in the life sciences. We're excited by this progress and look forward to sharing what comes next. Acknowledgements This research is led by Annalisa Pawlosky, alongside Pooja Rao and Petar Sirkovic. We would like to thank our co-authors and collaborators across the foundational papers supporting this work: Zach Cutts, John Coller, Rachel Chen, Mathias Bellaiche, Hua Tang, Ryder Easterlin, and Dina Zverinski (aptamer discovery); Jun Kim, Artiom Myaskovsky, Oscar Donosa, Jamie Rogers, and Lawrence Chan (protein design); and Yves Delley, John Coller, Zach Cutts, Alexander Daryin, Mathias Bellaiche, Jun Kim, Oscar Donosa, Srinidhi Seshadri, Tanner Clary, and Sandy Klemm, with additional technical and experimental contributions from Xinyi Deng, Sanath Ramachandran and Jiawu Bi (VERID automation). We are deeply grateful to Reuven Sayag, Avinatan Hassidim, Ronit Levavi Morad, Yossi Matias, and James Manyika for their leadership guidance and to Matthias Heiler, Burak Gokturk, Bill Jia and Pushmeet Kohli for their support throughout this research. We also thank Shekoofeh Azizi, Andrew Carroll, Philip Q. Nelson, Yishay Mansour, Dan Popovici, and Riccardo Pisoni for their reviews and insightful feedback, Amanie Brik for overall contributions to the effort, and Udi Graff for visual design and graphics for this post. items.title: Welcome Beam: a 501B open model you can own, customize, and scale
items.content: Back to Articles a]:hidden"> Welcome Beam: a 501B open model you can own, customize, and scale Published October 16, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 60 +54 ben burtenshaw burtenshaw Follow merve merve Follow Pedro Cuenca pcuenq Follow :last-child]:mb-0"> Beam by Reflection is out on Hugging Face! It is the first model from the new US lab, Reflection, and it’s open! It's a mixture-of-experts (MoEs) model with 501B parameters (23B active per token), supports text as input, has a context window of 1M tokens , and is released under the Apache 2.0 license. Beam is focused on coding and agentic use cases. It is for teams that want a frontier-scale model on their own hardware, infrastructure, or cloud, and want to customize it to their own use cases. Beam ships with its own dedicated open source Rust based harness that delivers the best performance from the model. Beam has a native transformers implementation, as well as downstream libraries like vLLM and SGLang. We’ve worked with the Reflection team to bring you inference, SFT (supervised fine tuning), and RL (reinforcement learning) recipes for you to build with this model for your needs. On top of day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM, this post shows you how to run it, how to post-train it, and what we built with it. TL;DR 501B-parameter MoEs LLM with 23B active per token. 52 layers, 256 experts per MoE layer, 8 routed per token. Text in, text out with context window of 1M tokens. Checkpoint formats: BF16 , FP8 , and NVFP4 Reasoning that can stay in context across turns ( preserve_thinking ), tool calling with a dedicated grammar. The model supports five reasoning values: "low", "medium" (default), "high", "xhigh", and "max". Response template in the tokenizer. Speculative decoding drafter model with DFlash2 Day-0 libraries: transformers, SGLang, vLLM. Full-parameter RL with Miles. Ships with a Rust-based custom harness. Apache 2.0. Build with Beam Reflection is going to give out $10,000 Hub credits to the best projects that use Beam. All you have to do is make a thing, and share it on the Hub: You could make a demo that uses the Beam model on Spaces You could quantize it for your favorite hardware You could generate a synthetic dataset for your favorite problem You could build an RL environment with or for Beam You could benchmark Beam and share the results. You could surprise us! If you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build the space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page . We’ll collect all the links, select the best, and send out the credits to your Hub accounts. What is Beam? Beam is a text-only model built for long-context (1M context length) reasoning and agentic work. It is a sparse MoE model, where each token is computed by a small fraction of the network, so it runs at the speed of a much smaller model while keeping the capacity of a large one. Attention The decoder has 52 layers with a hidden size of 5,120. Most layers use sliding-window attention over the previous 512 tokens; every sixth layer, and the last one, attend to the full context. That gives 43 sliding-window layers and 9 global ones. Inside the attention block (both layer types) The two kinds of layers handle position differently. Sliding-window layers use RoPE, since relative position matters most within a short window. Global layers use no positional encoding . Instead, each query is multiplied by a scaler that grows slowly with the number of visible tokens, (1 + (pos + 1) / 2048) ** 0.1 . It acts as a temperature: the softmax keeps its precision as the context lengthens instead of flattening out. The implementation calls this scalable-softmax query scaling. Attention uses grouped-query attention with 48 query heads and 8 key-value heads, with RMSNorm on queries and keys. A learned sigmoid gate, computed from the layer input, scales every channel of every head before the output projection. Mixture of Experts The first 3 layers use a dense SwiGLU MLP. The other 49 replace it with a Mixture-of-Experts block of 256 experts, each a SwiGLU MLP with an intermediate size of 2,560, or about 39M parameters. The experts hold 98.4% of the model's parameters. The router follows DeepSeek-V3's group-limited scheme. It scores all 256 experts with a sigmoid, splits them into 8 groups of 32, keeps the 4 best groups (ranked by the sum of each group's top two scores), then picks the top 8 experts inside them. Beam uses the same group sizes as DeepSeek-V3 but no shared expert. Expert outputs are combined with normalized router weights and scaled by 2.5. Only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 23B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of a 501B model but runs at the speed of a 23B one. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores most parameters in 4-bit precision for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs, some parameters are kept in BF16 for accuracy. There are also FP8 checkpoints on the hub which are ideal for Hopper and Ampere series chips. If you want to deploy Beam yourself, check out the vLLM or SGLang recipes below. Residual Stream The residual connections are the most distinctive part. A standard transformer adds each sublayer output to the stream with weight 1, so the stream grows with depth. Beam counts the input embedding as step 1. At step k it adds the sublayer output with weight 1/sqrt(k) and keeps the existing stream with weight sqrt((k-1)/k) . The squares of the two weights sum to one, so the stream stays at a constant scale from the first layer to the last. After all 104 additions, every sublayer output and the input embedding carry the same weight in the final hidden state. Every sublayer is also normalized before and after, and the final logits pass through a tanh softcap at ±30, computed in FP32. The implementation fixes where it computes in FP32: the router, the SwiGLU product, the norms, RoPE, the query scaling and the softcap. Long Context Hybrid attention works well for long contexts. Each layer caches 2 x 8 KV heads x 128 dims = 2,048 values per token. If all 52 layers kept every token, the cache would grow by 208 KiB per token. Only the 9 global layers keep the whole sequence. The 43 sliding-window layers hold a fixed 512-token window each and stop growing. So the cache grows by 36 KiB per token, roughly a sixth of the naive rate. Context If all 52 layers were global Beam 32K tokens 6.5 GiB 1.2 GiB 128K tokens 26 GiB 4.6 GiB Full context (1M) 208 GiB 36.08 GiB These numbers are per sequence, in BF16, with the transformers dynamic cache. Benchmark Results Here are the benchmark results across different precision levels, as provided by the Reflection team. Beam (BF16) Beam (FP8) Beam (NVFP4) Agentic Coding / Terminal DeepSWE v1.1 43.3% 43.0% 42.7% SWE Bench Pro v2-Hard 76.5% 78.4% 78.6% SWE Bench Pro v1 66.1% 65.9% 65.6% Terminal Bench v2.1 80.1% 78.9% 78.2% SWE Atlas Codebase QnA 31.8% 32.2% 31.4% SWEBench Multilingual 78.3% 78.1% 77.5% SWEBench Verified 81.6% 80.2% 80.7% Reasoning AIME 2026 97.7% 98.0% 97.5% HLE (no tools) 36.0% 36.0% 34.8% HLE (with tools) 51.1% 51.1% 51.1% SciCode 49.2% 48.3% 46.9% CriPT AA 16.3% 17.4% 15.4% GPQA Diamond 90.6% 90.3% 89.3% LiveCodeBench 88.3% 88.1% 87.4% Tool Calling / Search AutomationBench - public split only 39.3 38.2 39.8% MCP Atlas 80.8% 81.5% 80.5% Tau3 Banking 36.1% 36.8% 35.4% BrowseComp w/ context management 76.8% 76.7% 75.6% DeepSearchQA w/ context management 80.5% 79.6% 81.1% General Capabilities AA-LCR 78.2% 79.4% 78.7% LongBench v2 67.5% 67.6% 67.2% IFBench 79.6% 80.7% 79.2% AA Omniscience (index) - public split only 10.8 8.8 9.8 Hardware Requirements The most practical way to serve the model is serving the NVFP4 checkpoint, which retains most of the quality of the bf16 checkpoint. NVFP4 stores some weights in 4 bits, and this way, it shrinks the 501B parameters in BF16 from 1 TB to ~280 GB. Blackwell GPUs run NVFP4 natively but GPUs older than Blackwell like the H200 can't. The FP8 checkpoints are suitable for GPUs older than Blackwell. A B200 has 180 GB of HBM3e, so two of them (360 GB) can hold the Beam weights, with little room left for activations and the KV cache. Plan for four B200s (720 GB), which leaves plenty of room for long contexts and concurrent requests. You can also serve it on a full 8xB200 node, or on two B300s at 288 GB each, or even 8xRTX Pro 6000. If you don't have Blackwell hardware, use Inference Providers (serverless) to test Reflection. Inference Support Beam comes with day-0 support in transformers, SGLang and vLLM. Transformers Install the latest version of transformers. pip install -U "transformers>=5.20.1" The easiest way to run Beam is the text-generation pipeline: from transformers import pipeline pipe = pipeline( "text-generation" , model= "reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B" , device_map= "auto" ) messages = [ { "role" : "user" , "content" : "Write a limerick about Python exceptions." } ] output = pipe(messages, max_new_tokens= 2000 ) output[ 0 ][ "generated_text" ][- 1 ] The pipeline returns the whole chat. The last message is Beam's reply, already parsed by the response template. Going one level lower, use AutoModelForCausalLM and AutoTokenizer . from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer model_id = "reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B" tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id) model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained( model_id, dtype= "auto" , device_map= "auto" ) Chat messages = [ { "role" : "system" , "content" : "You should only answer with a number." }, { "role" : "user" , "content" : "What is 17 * 23?" }, ] inputs = tokenizer.apply_chat_template( messages, add_generation_prompt= True , tokenize= True , return_dict= True , return_tensors= "pt" , reasoning_effort= "medium" # by default ).to(model.device) input_len = inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[- 1 ] outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens= 2000 ) tokenizer.parse_response( outputs[ 0 ][input_len:], prefix=inputs[ "input_ids" ][ 0 ] ) Beam's tokenizer carries a response template. parse_response reads it and turns the raw output into a message dict, with the reasoning, the answer, and any tool calls in separate fields. This avoids the usual regex for splitting reasoning from answers from tool calls. And the rules ship with the tokenizer, so the parsed structure matches what Beam was trained to produce. The chat template can pre-write part of the assistant turn, which the parser needs to see. Tool calling Complete tool-calling example def get_weather ( city: str , unit: str = "celsius" ): """ Get the current weather for a city. Args: city: The city to look up. unit: Temperature unit, "celsius" or "fahrenheit". """ ... tools = [get_weather] messages = [ { "role" : "user" , "content" : "I land in Paris tonight. Do I need a coat?" } ] inputs = tokenizer.apply_chat_template( messages, tools=tools, add_generation_prompt= True , tokenize= True , return_dict= True , return_tensors= "pt" , ).to(model.device) input_len = inputs[ "input_ids" ].shape[- 1 ] outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens= 1000 ) message = tokenizer.parse_response( outputs[ 0 ][input_len:], prefix=inputs[ "input_ids" ][ 0 ], tools=tools ) message.get( "tool_calls" ) Pass tools to parse_response as well. Beam writes tool-call arguments inline, in its own XML-style grammar, so a bare 7 could be a number or a string. With the tool schemas, the parser casts each argument to its declared type. Multi-GPU and multi-node Beam's config defines an expert-parallel plan. Expert parallelism puts each expert on one device. Attention, the dense layers, the embeddings and the LM head are replicated on every device. That is 8B parameters, or 16 GB in BF16. Load the model with a DistributedConfig : import os from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM from transformers.distributed import DistributedConfig model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained( "reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B" , distributed_config=DistributedConfig( tp_size= int (os.environ[ "WORLD_SIZE" ]), ep_size= int (os.environ[ "WORLD_SIZE" ]), tp_plan={} ), ) Launch the script with torchrun across 16 H200 GPUs. Each one then holds 78 GB of weights. With 8 GPUs each would hold 139 GB, which leaves no room on a 141 GB H200. The number of devices must divide the number of experts, 256. vLLM Beam has day-0 support in vLLM. The command below serves the BF16 checkpoint with tensor parallelism across 16 GPUs (two 8x H200 nodes) and exposes an OpenAI-compatible API: vllm serve reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B --tensor-parallel-size 16 --served-model-name beam For faster generation, add DFlash2 speculative decoding. A small drafter model proposes up to 15 tokens ahead, and Beam checks them all in one forward pass, so each step can accept several tokens. The cost is a little extra memory for the drafter: vllm serve reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B \ --tensor-parallel-size 16 \ --speculative-config '{ "method": "dflash", "model": "reflection/dflash2-drafter-preview", "num_speculative_tokens": 15 }' Both commands start an OpenAI-compatible server, so you can point any OpenAI client at http://localhost:8000/v1 . For additional serving configurations, see the proposed Beam recipe for vLLM . SGLang Beam also has day-0 support in SGLang. We recommend serving it with DFlash2 speculative decoding, which both commands below turn on. On Blackwell, the NVFP4 checkpoint fits on 4 B300s: python -m sglang.launch_server \ --model-path reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B-NVFP4 \ --served-model-name beam \ --tp 4 \ --attention-backend trtllm_mha \ --page-size 64 \ --context-length 1048576 \ --mem-fraction-static 0.85 \ --enable-unified-memory \ --speculative-algorithm DFLASH \ --speculative-draft-model-path reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B-DFlash2 \ --speculative-dflash-block-size 8 \ --tool-call-parser beam --reasoning-parser beam \ --host 0.0.0.0 --port 30000 On Hopper GPUs, use the FP8 checkpoint on 8 H200s instead. Only three flags change: the checkpoint, the tensor-parallel size (8 instead of 4), and the attention backend (fa3 instead of trtllm_mha, which needs Blackwell): python -m sglang.launch_server \ --model-path reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B-FP8 \ --served-model-name beam \ --tp 8 \ --attention-backend fa3 \ --page-size 64 \ --context-length 1048576 \ --mem-fraction-static 0.85 \ --enable-unified-memory \ --speculative-algorithm DFLASH \ --speculative-draft-model-path reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B-DFlash2 \ --speculative-dflash-block-size 8 \ --tool-call-parser beam --reasoning-parser beam \ --host 0.0.0.0 --port 30000 Inference Providers Beam is available on Hugging Face Inference Providers, powered by Baseten, Fireworks, and Together, with more to follow soon. import os from openai import OpenAI client = OpenAI( base_url= "https://router.huggingface.co/v1" , api_key=os.environ[ "HF_TOKEN" ], ) completion = client.chat.completions.create( model= "reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B:auto" , messages=[{ "role" : "user" , "content" : "What is the capital of France?" }], ) print (completion.choices[ 0 ].message) Inference Endpoints We’ve set up a Beam recipe for you to one click deploy in Inference Endpoints from the catalog in FP8 or NVFP4 , or install with the hf cli like so: hf endpoints catalog deploy --repo reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B --name beam What we tested We are sharing some vibe evals of Reflection Beam-501B-A23B on five tasks, once each at low and high reasoning effort through the Reflection platform. These are vibe evals, not benchmarks. If you’re planning on using Beam, this is a great way to kick the tires and see how it behaves on specific use cases, and importantly, where it wins and loses. Below is an overview of the prompts we ran and the output traces from the hub. The complete inputs, outputs, API usage, task fixtures, graders and conversation traces are in this public Hugging Face bucket . Category Prompt Description Low reasoning (tokens) High reasoning (tokens) Multi-step tool calling Fulfill ORD-742: compare stock, reservations, surcharges and arrival dates; reserve the cheapest eligible warehouse. ✅ 544 ✅ 811 Long-context retrieval over a code base Derive Click command configuration and two invocation results from three complete source files; cite six implementation symbols. 🔴 1,613 * ✅ 5,007 Terminal task in a sandbox Inspect and repair a CSV ledger CLI; fix all bugs, preserve tests, run tests and a CLI check. ✅ 582 ✅ 1,548 Math reasoning (AIME-style) How many eight-element subsets of {1, …, 16} have a sum divisible by 17? Give a justification. 🟠 829 † ✅ 2,809 Structured output Convert an out-of-order revision log into strict JSON: merge patches, cancellations, nulls, dates, currencies and totals. ✅ 1,040 ✅ 2,088 * Low's long-context response got all code behavior and all six source citations correct. However, the response did not correspond to the parsers format, so this is partly prompt ambiguity. † Low returned the correct answer, but omitted the requested justification. High supplied a correct roots-of-unity proof, independently reviewed. Don’t take our word for it. Dig into the bucket , rewrite for your use case or project and push Beam to the limit. Post-training Beam You can fine tune Beam for your own use cases. Here, we share some examples in TRL and Miles to get you started on supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning. SFT with TRL The quickest way to adapt Beam to your own data is supervised fine-tuning with TRL's SFTTrainer. To keep memory manageable, we train LoRA adapters with PEFT rather than updating all 501B parameters: We used TRL’s SFTTrainer to adapt Beam to a simple goal: keep its reasoning in the language requested by the user. We fine-tuned on Multilingual-Thinking with LoRA, which trains a small set of adapter weights while keeping the base model frozen. The setup combines model sharding at load time, expert parallelism, FlashAttention 4 and sequence packing. LoRA SFT fits on a single node with 8 B300 GPUs, reaching around 19,000 tokens per second. The corresponding H100 setup uses four nodes. After one epoch of Multilingual-Thinking, Beam reasoned in the requested language on 16 out of 16 held-out prompts, compared with 3 out of 16 for the base model. This small evaluation measures language adherence, rather than the correctness of the reasoning itself. Training loss (left) and mean token accuracy (right) during a separate 500-step run on a reasoning subset of open-r1/Mixture-of-Thought, using one 8-GPU B300 node. These training metrics are from the official TRL example PR . GRPO with Miles Reflection and RadixArk built a recipe that trains the model with GRPO in Miles, in BF16. You can update the full model or use LoRA to train adapters while keeping the base weights frozen. Megatron trains, SGLang generates the rollouts, and Miles publishes the new weights to the rollout engines after each update. We reviewed the recipe. Workload Reference configuration Inference / eval, BF16 16x H200 per engine Full-parameter GRPO, BF16 (Miles) 96x H200: 64 train, 32 rollout. Or 64x H200 colocated. LoRA GRPO, BF16 (Miles) 32x H200: 16 train, 16 rollout. Full-parameter GRPO, BF16, 128-token context (Miles) 48x H200: 32 train, 16 rollout. The setup Reflection and RadixArk first validated on the real checkpoint. The recipe runs GRPO on DAPO-Math-17K and evaluates on AIME25. Build the image, download the data, and submit the job to a Ray cluster of twelve 8x H200 nodes: docker build -f docker/Dockerfile.beam -t miles-beam . python scripts/run_beam.py prepare \ --model-id reflection/Beam-1.0-501B-A23B \ --model-dir /root/models/Beam \ --data-dir /data/datasets export MASTER_ADDR=10.0.0.1 export RAY_ADDRESS=http:// ${MASTER_ADDR} :8265 python scripts/run_beam.py execute \ --model-dir /root/models/Beam \ --data-dir /data/datasets \ --output-dir /root/shared_data/beam-run \ --num-rollout 100 What happens in a rollout: Sample: 32 prompts are passed to the model with 8 responses each. Two SGLang engines serve the rollouts on 16 GPUs each. Score: the boxed answer is checked against the label, with a soft penalty for responses near the length limit. Update: one optimizer step on all 256 samples. Group-relative advantages with truncated importance sampling, no KL or entropy penalty. Train in parallel: tensor parallelism 8, expert parallelism 8, data parallelism 8, with sequence parallelism and full recompute. Optimizer: Adam at a constant 1e-6. Gradients in BF16, master weights in FP32, moments in BF16. The optimizer state streams through node-local NVMe, so each trainer node needs 2 TB of scratch. Evaluate: AIME25 every five rollouts, eight samples per problem. A checkpoint is saved every twenty. The next rollout is generated while the current one trains, so responses are one update behind. Add --resume to continue from the last checkpoint. execute-colocate runs the same recipe on eight nodes, with every GPU training and serving in turn. Train with LoRA You can also run GRPO with LoRA on four 8× H200 nodes: 16 GPUs for training and 16 for rollouts. The recipe trains rank-16 adapters on Beam’s attention, dense MLP, and expert layers while keeping the base weights frozen. Only adapter weights are synchronized with SGLang, and the optimizer state stays in GPU memory, removing the need for NVMe optimizer offloading. python scripts/run_beam_lora.py execute \ --model-dir /root/models/Beam \ --data-dir /data/datasets \ --output-dir /root/shared_data/beam-run \ --num-rollout 100 Build with Beam: Demos If you build something with Beam, then share it on the Hub for a chance to win $10,000. All you have to do is build a space, model, or dataset repo and share it on the model’s repo page . To inspire you, here are a few things we built. Hey Beam, build a native local MacOS application! At Hugging Face we love open and local models that run native to their hardware, but building native apps on Mac can be hard! Let’s see if Beam can help us out. We asked Beam to build a native MacOS application that turns speech to text, and conveniently drops it at your cursor. We want to use MLX to get the most out of our Mac Metal and the Parakeet Model for great speech-to-text. Build BeamSpeak, a native macOS menu bar dictation app with a compact recording pill and no main window or account. Use ⌘⇧Space to start and stop microphone recording, showing elapsed time, microphone level, and transcription status. Run speech recognition entirely locally using a Hugging Face model, preferably Parakeet v3 through MLX, and keep the model loaded between recordings. Paste the transcript into the original app if it remains focused and Accessibility permission is granted; otherwise copy it to the clipboard, preserving newer clipboard changes and never pressing Enter. Handle permissions, cancellation, silence, errors, a two-minute recording limit, and temporary audio cleanup. Deliver source code, a runnable BeamSpeak.app, setup instructions, and verification of offline transcription, the physical shortcut, microphone capture, and text delivery. We used Beam with the Pi coding harness to build the initial native macOS menu bar app, running Parakeet with MLX. The saved run includes follow-up prompts; the final source also includes later Codex repairs. The prompt above is a condensed version of the build requirements. You can check out the agent trace of how Beam built this in pi in this trace . If you want to try the demo out, download the source code or read the setup instructions . Hey Beam, how do you scale on multiple agents? We wanted to see whether Beam could make faster progress by splitting a programming task across agents. We paired Beam with the open-source Pi coding agent and compared three setups: 1. one agent working alone, 2. five persistent peers collaborating through a shared Git repository, and 3. a lead agent delegating work to asynchronous subagents. The harness ran on Hugging Face jobs with inference through Reflection’s platform API. For the tasks, we used ProgramBench: agents must recreate a program from its compiled executable and documentation, without seeing its source code or the evaluator’s tests. Each setup had the same 8M API-token ceiling and two-hour solver limit per task, shared across its agents. We saved implementation snapshots and evaluated them against fixed hidden-test suites from the ProgramBench-Tests dataset . Our score-versus-latency plot shows the average fraction of tests passed. The time axis uses fixed reference rates for model tokens plus measured tool time, rather than elapsed wall time. We initially ran five tasks. The current figure shows a post-hoc subset of jq, xsv, FIGlet, and hexyl; ripgrep was excluded across all three setups because grading its saved artifacts was too slow. The published results retain all 15 original episodes. You can inspect the runs in the Trackio dashboard , explore the published result data , and reuse the study harness . Hey Beam, finetune a decision model for my code base! Decision models are all the rage at the moment because they’re super fast and practical for many use cases. We started with Beam in Pi after Beam’s quota ran out to train and evaluate a custom decision model for developer incident triage. We wanted to see whether a coding agent could turn an incident-triage policy into a small, fast decision model. The task was to read a developer incident and choose the responsible team, its severity, and whether someone should be pinged immediately. Using Unsloth, we fine-tuned Qwen3.5-0.8B to score these choices directly. First, the workflow built a synthetic dataset containing 2.3k incidents split by incident cluster for training, calibration, and testing. We trained a LoRA adapter and decision head for three epochs, with a 4-bit backbone, on one H100 80GB on the Science Slurm cluster. For a baseline, we prompted the unadapted model with the full triage policy and ticket, without examples, and asked it to generate the three decisions as JSON. On the same 320 synthetic test tickets, the fine-tuned decision model got all three answers correct on 76.25%, versus 4.69% for prompted zero-shot. Mean ticket latency fell from 1,218.06 ms to 102.58 ms, an 11.9× speedup. If you want to try out this experiment for yourself, check out the artifact bucket which contains the data, code, checkpoints and results. Wrapping Up Beam is a 501B open model that you can run on your own hardware and change. Start with the BF16 checkpoint, or try one of the quants FP8 , NVFP4 . If you build something with Beam, share it in the discussions tab . keyTakeaways: It is the first model from the new US lab, Reflection, and it’s open!
It's a mixture-of-experts (MoEs) model with 501B parameters (23B active per token), supports text as input, has a context window of 1M
Beam is focused on coding and agentic use cases.
