items.fingerprint: how specializing the vocabulary of slms can cut inference cost by 77 in real applications|huggingface.co/blog/dharma-ai
items.title: How Specializing the Vocabulary of SLMs Can Cut Inference Cost by 77% in Real Applications
items.content: Back to Articles a]:hidden"> How Specializing the Vocabulary of SLMs Can Cut Inference Cost by 77% in Real Applications Team Article Published October 21, 2026 Upvote 35 +29 Bernardo França de Aguiar bernardoaguiar Follow Dharma-AI Gabriel Pimenta de Freitas Cardoso GabrielPimenta99 Follow Dharma-AI Bruno Duarte brunoduarte01 Follow Dharma-AI Francisco de Almeida Rocha Alves falves9101 Follow Dharma-AI :last-child]:mb-0"> Models specialized for a domain or a task by fine-tuning general open-source models, such as Qwen and Gemma, inherit a vocabulary built for many domains and general applications. In an essay grader we run in production, that vocabulary split the text the model writes most into many tokens. This article previews some results from the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon: how we specialized the vocabulary around the cost of each token rather than its frequency, and cut measured inference cost by 77% without changing the base model. The tokenizer is usually treated as a fixed property of the base model, inherited and left alone. For a model specialized in a single domain, it can be one of the largest cost levers, and it is set before any training step. One of the systems we run in production is an automated grader for Portuguese essays, built on Qwen3-4B. It receives the essay, the prompt and the supporting texts, and returns a JSON assessment with a grade and a comment for each competency. The model was already small, at 4 billion parameters, and had already been trained for the task. Its tokenizer, however, was still the original Qwen3-4B one, built for many languages and many kinds of text. In the grader, it was used for a single language, Portuguese, and a single response format. That had two costs: the text the grader writes on every request took more tokens than it needed, and at every generated token the model scored a vocabulary of 151,669 entries, including many this task almost never uses. We rebuilt that vocabulary with a method we call VocabX, keeping the same base model, the same data and the same training recipe. The numbers in this article come from the current version of the paper, still under review, and may change before publication. A Vocabulary Built for Everyone The leading language models read and write in tokens, and the tokenizer decides how text becomes tokens. The tokenizers of the leading general-purpose models are trained on large collections of text from many domains and languages, from source code to contracts to Chinese. For a general-purpose model, that choice makes sense. For a model used in a single domain, it creates two kinds of waste at once. The first is fragmentation. The tokenizer splits into many pieces exactly what the domain repeats most. In the grader, every response starts with the same JSON envelope, the same competency names, the same evaluation phrases. In contracts, it is the boilerplate clauses. In code, the identifiers. Each of these sequences costs several tokens where one would do, and the model pays for every one of them on every request. The second is excess. The vocabulary carries tens of thousands of entries the domain never uses, and the model computes a score for all of them at every token it generates. A model tuned to grade American school biology exams will almost never write in Chinese, yet it computes the probability of every Chinese-language token at every step. The vocabulary splits into many pieces what the domain repeats most, and carries entries the domain never uses. Reading Is Cheap, Writing Is Expensive The natural reaction is to count tokens and try to reduce the count. But the count is not the bill. To see why a generated token costs more, it helps to look at how inference works. It has two phases. In prefill , the model processes the whole input in a single pass through the network: each weight read from GPU memory is reused for every input token, and the limit is compute. In decode , the model generates the response one token at a time, and each token needs a full pass. Each weight read is used only a few times, and the GPU spends most of its time waiting for data to arrive from memory: the limit becomes memory bandwidth. This effect is strongest exactly where we operate: small models served with moderate batches. Batching requests splits the weight reads across them and eases the problem, but does not solve it. At every decode step, the model also reads the KV cache, the attention memory that holds the context already processed and grows with it. In the case we measured, the grader, a generated token costs 7.4 times a token read, but the ratio varies with the hardware, the problem, the batch size, the context length and other factors, and it can be larger than that. In general, the direction holds: generating costs more than reading. Think of a shipping company that charges per box, but charges seven times more for outgoing boxes than for incoming ones. Reducing the total number of boxes helps. Reducing the outgoing boxes helps seven times more. A method that compresses input and output equally misses most of the possible savings. The third component of the bill is the vocabulary itself. The model's last layer, the LM head, turns the internal state into a score for every possible token. To do that, it holds one row of parameters per vocabulary entry. In a model the size of Qwen3-4B, that matrix accounts for almost 10% of the parameters. It is a share that large models absorb without noticing, but it weighs on a small model. And the cost is not paid only once. The input layer looks up only the row of the token being read, but the LM head reads and multiplies the entire matrix for every generated token. Since decode is already memory-bound, every extra row is more data to move at every step. An entry the domain never uses costs exactly the same as a frequent one. That is why adding tokens can lower the count and raise the bill at the same time. VocabX does not include this term in its selection criterion, but it controls vocabulary size in two steps: the sub-word merge replaces the base vocabulary with a smaller, domain-specific one, and macros enter under a fixed budget. In the grader, the output layer went from about 152,000 to about 65,000 rows. Why Existing Solutions Fell Short Adapting a model's vocabulary is not a new idea. Reference methods in the literature, such as fast vocabulary transfer (FVT), multi-word tokenization (MWT) and Liquid AI's in-place tokenizer expansion (in-place BPE), which continues BPE training from the original vocabulary, already reduce fragmentation. When we tested them on our problem, we found two limitations. They choose tokens by frequency, not by cost. An expression that appears often in the input is worth more to them than one that appears less often in the response, even if the second is the more expensive one to serve. They work on a single layer. They either adjust how words are cut into pieces, or merge whole phrases into one token. None of these three does both under the same criterion. And the grader's biggest waste was precisely in long, repeated spans such as the JSON envelope, which a sub-word method only reaches after merging each part, one by one. How We Solved It VocabX addresses both limitations, plus a third problem that appears on the obvious path to solving the first. First, we changed the question. Instead of asking how many tokens a candidate saves, we ask how much cost and time it saves. Each eliminated token is multiplied by the price of the field it appears in: system prompt, user message or model response. In the case we measured, the grader, a token saved in the response is worth 7.4 times one saved in the input, and the vocabulary is built accordingly. Second, we work on both layers at once. Back to the shipping company: you can cut boxes by packing each item better, or by recognizing that the same twelve-item kit ships every week and sending the kit in a single box. VocabX does both. At the sub-word layer, it rebuilds how domain words are cut into pieces. At the multi-word layer, it looks for whole spans that repeat, from short expressions to full lines and JSON envelopes, and turns each into a single token, which we call a macro token. Both layers are chosen under the same cost criterion, each with its own budget. To find these spans, we use five miners, automatic searches for spans that repeat across the corpus, each specialized in one kind of repetition: long words, whole lines, expressions, complete sentences, and structures with punctuation such as JSON and tags. Averaged over eight corpora, the last one contributed the most, and on code it alone accounted for 17.5 points. Without all five, token reduction on the grader would drop by 55.6 points. Third, we estimate what the sample cannot see. Choosing tokens by cost requires knowing how much each candidate still saves after the ones already chosen. Measuring that exactly would require reprocessing the entire corpus after every choice, tens of thousands of times. A common way to do this at scale is to measure on a sample of documents, and then a candidate absent from the sample gets zero gain. An expression that appears 37 times in 50,000 documents shows up in a 400-document sample only about 26% of the time. In a contracts corpus, only 16.6% of the candidates appear in a 400-document sample; the rest are never evaluated. A candidate's gain has two parts. One is how much it saves over the entire corpus, and that can be counted exactly, without a sample. The other is how much of that saving is not yet covered by the tokens already chosen, and only that part needs to be estimated. For candidates the sample cannot see, we use a statistical estimate based on the behavior of the ones it can see, instead of zero. A candidate that is rare in the sample but frequent in the corpus is back in the running. That change alone, with the same sample and the same budget, raised token reduction on a contracts corpus from 44.7% to 52.8%. What Changed in the Grader To measure the real effect, we trained seven versions of the grader with the same base model, the same data, the same recipe and the same seed. The only difference between them is the tokenizer. All of them ran the same 500 requests on the same test machine, with an RTX 5090 GPU and the vLLM inference server, and cost was calculated from measured runtime. The model's response dropped from 350 to 101 tokens on average. Cost dropped 77.0%. Quality, measured by the bench score, which combines grading accuracy and the accuracy of screening off-topic or rule-breaking essays, rose from 0.703 to 0.810. Getting there required a course correction. The first version of the vocabulary fused each competency's grade with the surrounding JSON into a single macro token. It was the most compact option, but quality dropped: its bench score was 0.689, below the production grader's 0.703. With the grade inside the macro, each combination of grade and structure became a different variant of the same token, and the model chose both in a single step. Giving the grade its own token cost 2 extra tokens per response, raised the bench score to 0.810 and, in the measurement, was even cheaper: a 77.0% reduction, against 73.3% for the fused version. The lesson applies beyond the grader. Compression has a cost when the compressed span carries the very decision the model exists to make. The goal is not the cheapest possible vocabulary, but the cheapest one that preserves the tokens that matter. Beyond the Grader To find out whether the gain was specific to our case, we compared VocabX with the three reference methods on five public domains (contracts, medical papers, scientific papers, news and Python code) and three model families (Qwen3, Llama-3.1 and Gemma-3). All methods used the same mining and test documents, and the same vocabulary ceiling. VocabX compressed more than the strongest reference method in all fifteen combinations, by 1.2 to 9.3 points. In estimated inference cost, the pruned version of VocabX also led in all fifteen, with average margins of 10.2 points on Qwen3, 7.5 on Llama-3.1 and 13.6 on Gemma-3. On contracts, the pruned version reached 62.6% token reduction with 113,426 vocabulary entries, against 61.8% for the best in-place BPE configuration, which uses 207,803. Paying Only for the Tokens That Matter VocabX does not make the model smarter. It makes the model stop paying for text it does not need to write piece by piece, and stop scoring a vocabulary it will never use. In our grader, that cut measured inference cost by 77%, with the same base model and the same training recipe. Specialization usually starts with data and weights. It can also start one layer earlier, in the vocabulary. The full method, the tables for every experiment and the discarded interventions will be in the VocabX paper, which we will publish soon. Sources Dharma-AI. "VocabX: Cost-Weighted Vocabulary Adaptation for Domain-Specific Language Models." In preparation (2026). Gee, Leonidas, et al. " Fast vocabulary transfer for language model compression ." EMNLP Industry Track (2022). Gee, Leonidas, et al. "Multi-word tokenization for sequence compression." EMNLP Industry Track (2023). Smith, Jimmy T.H., et al. " In-Place Tokenizer Expansion for Pre-trained LLMs ." arXiv:2607.15232 (2026). items.title: Welcome FLUX.3 Image Klein in Diffusers
items.content: Back to Articles a]:hidden"> Welcome FLUX.3 Image Klein in Diffusers: The latest open image generation model from Black Forest Labs Published October 15, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 49 +43 Aritra Roy Gosthipaty ariG23498 Follow Sayak Paul sayakpaul Follow Linoy Tsaban linoyts Follow :last-child]:mb-0"> Black Forest Labs FLUX.3 Image Klein is here, and it runs in Diffusers from day one. One model does text-to-image and multi-reference image-to-image, and it adds something new, the layout control . You write bounding boxes into the prompt to say where each part of the image should go, or which parts of a reference image to move. Both open checkpoints are in the FLUX.3 Image Klein collection : Checkpoint What it is Defaults black-forest-labs/flux-3-image-klein Time step distilled, for fast inference 16 steps, no CFG black-forest-labs/flux-3-image-klein-base Base model 50 steps, CFG You can head on to the Hugging Face space and generate some images right now! TL;DR One model for text-to-image, multi-reference image-to-image, and bounding-box layout control. The distilled checkpoint makes a 1024 × 1024 image in about 2 seconds on an H100. NVFP4 and FP8 weights load with from_single_file , for smaller GPUs. LoRA training scripts for both text-to-image and image editing. Ships as a Modular Diffusers pipeline, so you can pop blocks out or add your own. Contents Getting started What FLUX.3 can do Base model and quantized variants LoRA finetuning What it costs to run The architecture Modular Diffusers Try it Getting started Install the latest diffusers and transformers (for the Qwen3-VL text encoder): pip install -U diffusers transformers Load the distilled checkpoint and generate an image: import torch from diffusers import ModularPipeline pipe = ModularPipeline.from_pretrained( "black-forest-labs/flux-3-image-klein" ) pipe.load_components(dtype=torch.bfloat16) pipe.to( "cuda" ) pipe(prompt= "a red fox" , output= "images" )[ 0 ].save( "fox.png" ) What FLUX.3 can do Text-to-image FLUX.3 responds best to a full scene description with the subject, the setting, the light, the composition, and the style. The official prompting guide from Black Forest Labs has more tips. The distilled checkpoint generates a 1024 × 1024 image in 16 steps by default. Pass height , width , or num_inference_steps to change them. prompt = ( "A wide-angle wildlife photograph of a red fox standing alert in a snow-covered forest clearing at golden hour. " "The fox is centered in the frame, its thick orange winter coat contrasting with the fresh white snow, breath " "visible in the cold air. Snow-laden pine trees fill the softly blurred background, and low warm sunlight rakes " "across the scene from the left, casting long blue shadows." ) fox = pipe( prompt=prompt, generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed( 0 ), output= "images" )[ 0 ] fox.save( "fox.png" ) Text to image Image-to-image Pass a reference image (or more) with the image argument. Write the prompt as a caption of the image you want , with the change included. prompt = ( "The same red fox in the same snow-covered forest clearing, now at night under a full moon: cool blue " "moonlight, deep shadows, stars visible through the pine branches, the fox's eyes catching the light." ) night = pipe( prompt=prompt, image=fox, # from the previous text to image example generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed( 0 ), output= "images" , )[ 0 ] night.save( "night.png" ) Image to image With several references, refer to them in the prompt as <ref_image_0> , <ref_image_1> , ... in the order they are passed to image : red_fox = pipe(prompt= "a red fox" , generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed( 0 ), output= "images" )[ 0 ] bench = pipe(prompt= "a wooden bench" , generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed( 0 ), output= "images" )[ 0 ] combined = pipe( prompt= "The fox from <ref_image_0> sitting on the wooden bench from <ref_image_1> in a snowy setting." , image=[red_fox, bench], output= "images" , )[ 0 ] combined.save( "combined.png" ) <ref_image_0> : a red fox <ref_image_1> : a wooden bench The fox on the bench Layout control Add a JSON list of regions after the caption. Each region has an id , a bbox , and a desc , and the caption mentions it as <id> . Boxes are written as [y_min, x_min, y_max, x_max] , y first , on a 0–1000 scale. Because the scale is normalized, the same box works at any image size. Placing regions in a new image layout_prompt = ( "Minimalist graphic illustration featuring a black silhouette of a person <silhouette_1> centered against a " "solid, vibrant chartreuse background <background_1>. The figure is captured in a dynamic, mid-stride running " "pose, facing toward the left side of the frame. " '[{"id": "background_1", "bbox": [0, 0, 1000, 1000], "desc": "A flat field of neon yellow-green with a subtle ' 'paper texture and fine, organic grain."}, {"id": "silhouette_1", "bbox": [150, 150, 850, 850], "desc": "A ' "black silhouette of a person in motion, made of dense stippled ink. The leading edges are solid; the trailing " 'arm and leg dissolve into coarse square pixels and scattered dots."}]' ) runner = pipe(prompt=layout_prompt, generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed( 0 ), output= "images" )[ 0 ] Each region's desc is drawn inside its bbox Moving regions within a reference image For edits, each region says where its content comes from ( src_bbox in the reference) and where it goes ( tgt_bbox in the output). A region with the same two boxes stays where it is. This example moves the knitted knight up and to the left, and pins the backdrop, the cliff, the needle, the dragon, and the fire: from diffusers.utils import load_image knight_image = load_image( "knight_orig.png" ) edit_prompt = ( "In <ref_image_0>, move the miniature grey amigurumi knight figure <knight_1> upwards and to the left along the " "yarn cliff <cliff_1>. Keep the rest of the image completely unchanged, preserving the blurred yarn backdrop " "<backdrop_1>, the large knitted dragon <dragon_1>, and the fiery orange thread <fire_1>. " '[{"id": "knight_1", "from": "ref_image_0", "src_bbox": [500, 150, 850, 350], "tgt_bbox": [194, 55, 544, 255], ' '"desc": "A miniature amigurumi knight crocheted from thick grey woolen yarn."}, ' '{"id": "backdrop_1", "from": "ref_image_0", "src_bbox": [0, 0, 1000, 1000], "tgt_bbox": [0, 0, 1000, 1000], ' '"desc": "A soft, out-of-focus backdrop of cream and indigo knitted yarn."}, ' '{"id": "cliff_1", "from": "ref_image_0", "src_bbox": [300, 0, 1000, 450], "tgt_bbox": [300, 0, 1000, 450], ' '"desc": "A steep cliff of stacked yarn skeins in mustard, terracotta, and indigo."}, ' '{"id": "needle_1", "from": "ref_image_0", "src_bbox": [420, 250, 550, 450], "tgt_bbox": [420, 250, 550, 450], ' '"desc": "An oversized polished steel tapestry needle."}, ' '{"id": "dragon_1", "from": "ref_image_0", "src_bbox": [100, 600, 950, 1000], "tgt_bbox": [100, 600, 950, 1000], ' '"desc": "A large, fluffy knitted dragon in terracotta and mustard yarn."}, ' '{"id": "fire_1", "from": "ref_image_0", "src_bbox": [350, 400, 650, 650], "tgt_bbox": [350, 400, 650, 650], ' '"desc": "Curled puffs of fiery orange angora thread suspended in mid-air."}]' ) moved = pipe(prompt=edit_prompt, image=knight_image, generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed( 0 ), output= "images" )[ 0 ] The knight moves from its src_bbox to its tgt_bbox , and the rest of the scene stays put Base model and quantized variants Base model Everything above uses the distilled checkpoint. The base checkpoint runs 50 steps with classifier-free guidance, and it's the one to fine-tune (see LoRA finetuning ). pipe = ModularPipeline.from_pretrained( "black-forest-labs/flux-3-image-klein-base" ) pipe.load_components(dtype={ "vae" : torch.float32, "default" : torch.bfloat16}) pipe.to( "cuda" ) pipe.guider = pipe.guider.new(guidance_scale= 5.0 ) # optional image = pipe(prompt=prompt, output= "images" )[ 0 ] Single-file format checkpoints Black Forest Labs also ships the transformer as a single file, in bf16 and in two quantized formats: fp8r (rowwise FP8) and nvfp4 . Load any of them with from_single_file , then load the other components by name so the bf16 transformer isn't downloaded too. from diffusers import BFLQuantizationConfig, Flux3Transformer2DModel, ModularPipeline model_id = "black-forest-labs/flux-3-image-klein-base" variant = "fp8r" # or "nvfp4" transformer = Flux3Transformer2DModel.from_single_file( f"https://huggingface.co/ {model_id} /blob/main/variants/ {variant} /model.safetensors" , config=model_id, subfolder= "transformer" , quantization_config=BFLQuantizationConfig(compute_dtype=torch.bfloat16), dtype=torch.bfloat16, ) pipe = ModularPipeline.from_pretrained(model_id) pipe.load_components(dtype=torch.bfloat16) pipe.update_components(transformer=transformer) pipe.to( "cuda" ) For the unquantized single file, use https://huggingface.co/{model_id}/blob/main/model.safetensors and drop quantization_config . Variant Fast kernels on Other GPUs fp8r Compute capability 8.9+ (Ada, Hopper, Blackwell) Weights are dequantized each step: lower memory, no speedup nvfp4 Blackwell, with flashinfer-python and flashinfer-cubin at the same version Same as above LoRA finetuning FLUX.3 works for both text-to-image and image-to-image, which makes it a great base for custom LoRAs. diffusers ships DreamBooth LoRA training scripts for both tasks (you can also train with Ostris' AI Toolkit ). Here is a text-to-image example that learns a tarot-card style from the multimodalart/1920-raider-waite-tarot-public-domain dataset, triggered with trtcrd : accelerate launch train_dreambooth_lora_flux3_klein.py \ --pretrained_model_name_or_path= "black-forest-labs/flux-3-image-klein-base" \ --dataset_name= "multimodalart/1920-raider-waite-tarot-public-domain" \ --caption_column= "caption" \ --instance_prompt= "trtcrd" \ --output_dir= "trained-flux3-tarot-lora" \ --mixed_precision= "bf16" \ --resolution=1024 \ --use_aspect_ratio_buckets \ --train_batch_size=1 \ --rank=16 \ --lora_alpha=16 \ --learning_rate=1e-4 \ --lr_scheduler= "constant" \ --max_train_steps=1500 \ --validation_prompt= "a trtcrd of a cat, tarot style" \ --validation_epochs=25 \ --seed=0 \ --push_to_hub To reduce memory usage, add a few optimization flags: --gradient_checkpointing \ --cache_latents \ --use_8bit_adam --gradient_checkpointing recomputes activations in the backward pass (lower VRAM, slightly slower), --cache_latents pre-encodes the images and frees the VAE, and --use_8bit_adam keeps the optimizer states in 8-bit. A couple of knobs are worth experimenting with. The grid below trains the same tarot style with different LoRA ranks and optimizers; the adapters are on the Hub at diffusers-modular/flux3-tarot-lora . More training features and configurations are documented in the DreamBooth FLUX.3 README . For instruction-based editing, the image-to-image script ( train_dreambooth_lora_flux3_klein_img2img.py ) trains on (reference image, target image, instruction) triplets, where the reference is addressed in the prompt as <ref_image_0> . See the DreamBooth FLUX.3 README for all options and the full image-to-image example. What it costs to run In this section, we will talk about the memory consumption and the speed of generation of the models. Memory name peak allocated (after load) GiBs peak allocated (after inference) GiBs nvfp4 (RTX6000) 13.4 15.3 fp8r (H100) 14.35 16.27 bf16 (H100) 18.80 20.72 If you have less memory: Load a quantized transformer . Run the text encoder separately and free it. It only runs once per image, before denoising (see Encode once, generate many ). Turn on automatic CPU offloading, which moves each component to the GPU only while it runs (we didn't benchmark this) from diffusers import ComponentsManager, ModularPipeline manager = ComponentsManager() manager.enable_auto_cpu_offload(device= "cuda" ) pipe = ModularPipeline.from_pretrained( "black-forest-labs/flux-3-image-klein" , components_manager=manager) pipe.load_components(dtype={ "vae" : torch.float32, "default" : torch.bfloat16}) # no pipe.to("cuda"): the manager handles device placement Speed End-to-end timings for the distilled checkpoint (16 steps), averaged over three runs after a warmup: Workflow Output size Time Peak memory Text-to-image 1024 × 1024 1.93 s 23.8 GiB Image-to-image, one 1024 × 1024 reference 1024 × 1024 3.87 s 23.8 GiB Layout editing (the knight), one 1360 × 768 reference 1360 × 768 4.10 s 23.8 GiB Single NVIDIA H100 80GB, no offloading, default attention backend. A reference image roughly doubles the time. Reference tokens join the same sequence as the text and the image being generated, so a 1024 × 1024 reference adds 4,096 tokens to every transformer call Stacked bars of tokens per transformer call: text-to-image 4,256 tokens; image-to-image 8,272; layout text-to-image 4,336; layout image-to-image 8,800 The architecture Let's open the model up, one piece at a time. The model takes three kinds of tokens: text the noisy image being generated and optional reference images From pixels to tokens FLUX.3 is a latent-space flow model for image generation. This means that the denoiser takes latents as inputs and produces latents as outputs. We use a VAE to decode the latents back to pixels. FLUX.3 uses the same VAE architecture as Flux.2. The FLUX.2 VAE compresses an image 8× in each direction into 32 channels, and then every 2 × 2 patch of that latent is packed into a single token with 128 channels. So one token covers a 16 × 16 pixel patch , and a 1024 × 1024 image becomes a 64 × 64 grid of 4,096 tokens. The noisy image starts as random noise of exactly that shape. A reference image goes through the same VAE encoder and packing, and keeps its own size. From prompt to tokens The text encoder is Qwen3-VL, a vision-language model. FLUX.3 doesn't just take its last layer. It reads the hidden states of eight of its 36 layers (layers 4, 8, …, 32) and stacks them, so each text token becomes a 8 × 2560 = 20,480-dimensional vector before a linear layer projects it to the transformer's width of 3072. This gives the transformer features from several depths of the language model, not just its final layer. The prompt is padded to a multiple of 80 tokens, and the transformer attends to the padding too, which is why the pipeline takes one prompt per call. Two stages The transformer processes the tokens in two stages: Stage 1: per-mode blocks. Each stream goes through 5 blocks with its own weights. Text has its own blocks, the noisy image has its own, and the reference images have their own. Stage 2: joint blocks. The streams are concatenated into one sequence, [text | image | reference] , which goes through 28 blocks that share one set of weights. The two stages differ in who can attend to whom . In stage 1, each stream only attends to itself, so each kind of token gets refined on its own terms first. In stage 2, everything attends to everything, where the image learns from the text and from the references. For comparison, FLUX.2's double-stream blocks also give text and image separate weights, but let them attend to each other from the start. FLUX.3 keeps the streams fully apart first, then merges them. At the end, the text and reference tokens are simply dropped. Only the image tokens go through the output layers, which predict how to move them one step toward a clean image. Inside one block Every block, in either stage, has the same shape. Attention and the MLP run in parallel on the same normalized input, and their sum is added back to the residual stream. Each block starts with a LayerNorm that has no learned scale or shift of its own. The scale, shift, and gate come from a timestep embedding instead (this is called modulation ). Inside the attention, the queries and keys are RMS-normalized and get rotary position embeddings (RoPE), which we look at below. In a joint block, all tokens share the same weights, but text, image, and reference tokens each get their own scale, shift, and gate. def block ( x, shift, scale, gate ): # shift, scale, gate come from the token's timestep embedding h = layer_norm(x) # no learned scale or shift h = ( 1 + scale) * h + shift q, k, v = to_q(h), to_k(h), to_v(h) q, k = rope(rms_norm(q)), rope(rms_norm(k)) out = attention(q, k, v) + mlp(h) # parallel, MLP is SwiGLU return x + gate * out Every token gets its own timestep In FLUX.1 and FLUX.2, one timestep embedding modulates every token. In FLUX.3, the modulation depends on the kind of token. The noisy image tokens are modulated by the current timestep t . The text and reference tokens are always modulated by timestep 0 , which means "clean, nothing to denoise here". So even a reference that looks almost the same as the output is marked as given context, not as something to generate. The distilled checkpoint is a flow map . It is also told the timestep each step jumps to. That second timestep gets its own embedding, which is added to every token's modulation, so each of its 16 steps can make a larger jump. Positions in four dimensions Attention on its own doesn't know where a token is (this phenomenon is called permutation equivariance). RoPE fixes that by rotating each query and key by an amount that depends on the token's position. FLUX.3 uses four position axes, (t, h, w, l) (timestep, height, width, length of sequence), and gives each one a quarter (32 dimensions) of every 128-dimensional attention head: Tokens t: timestep h: height w: width l: length of sequence text token i 0 0 0 i image token at (row, col) 0 row / 2 col / 2 0 reference k at (row, col) 0 row / 2 col / 2 −( k + 1) Text tokens line up along l , like words in a sentence. The image and the references are 2D grids in (h, w) , separated from each other along l . Because a reference uses the same (h, w) coordinates as the output, "the same spot in the reference" has a precise meaning to the model, which is what the src_bbox / tgt_bbox editing relies on. The denoising loop FLUX.3 is a flow-matching model. Generation starts from pure noise, and at each of the 50 steps the transformer predicts a velocity . This is the direction from noise toward a clean image. The scheduler takes one step along it. At every step you can also read off the model's current guess of the final image. Decoding that guess at a few steps shows how the image takes shape: Step 1 Step 5 Step 10 Step 15 Step 25 Step 50 The fox, its pose, and the light are already in place by step 10, while the noise level is still 0.97. The snow-laden branches and the texture of the fur only appear in the last few steps. FLUX.3's scheduler uses a large time shift (6.93), which keeps the noise level high for most of the run: 44 of the 50 steps happen above σ = 0.5. We built this figure by adding one small block to the pipeline, which brings us to Modular Diffusers. If you are new to flow matching, we have a beginner friendly tutorial and a video for you to understand how it works. Modular Diffusers FLUX.3 ships as a Modular Diffusers pipeline. See the workflows You can list the workflows and print the exact blocks of each one, without loading any weights. from diffusers import Flux3AutoBlocks blocks = Flux3AutoBlocks() print (blocks.available_workflows) # ['text2image', 'image_conditioned'] print ( list (blocks.get_workflow( "text2image" ).sub_blocks)) # ['text_encoder', 'denoise.input', 'denoise.prepare_latents', 'denoise.set_timesteps', # 'denoise.prepare_rope_inputs', 'denoise.denoise', 'denoise.after_denoise', 'decode'] get_workflow() resolves the auto branches and gives you the plain sequence of steps that will run. print(blocks.get_workflow("image_conditioned").doc) prints the components, inputs, defaults, and outputs of that workflow. Encode once, generate many Pop the text encoder out, encode the prompt once, free it, and generate from the cached embeddings. import torch from diffusers import ModularPipeline model_id = "black-forest-labs/flux-3-image-klein-base" blocks = ModularPipeline.from_pretrained(model_id).blocks text_blocks = blocks.sub_blocks.pop( "text_encoder" ) # `blocks` now starts at the VAE encoder text_pipe = text_blocks.init_pipeline(model_id) text_pipe.load_components(dtype=torch.bfloat16) text_pipe.to( "cuda" ) state = text_pipe(prompt=prompt, negative_prompt= "" ) # no guider here, so ask for the negative embeddings prompt_embeds = state.get( "prompt_embeds" ) negative_prompt_embeds = state.get( "negative_prompt_embeds" ) del text_pipe torch.cuda.empty_cache() image_pipe = blocks.init_pipeline(model_id) # no text encoder to load image_pipe.load_components(dtype={ "vae" : torch.float32, "default" : torch.bfloat16}) image_pipe.to( "cuda" ) for seed in range ( 3 ): image = image_pipe( prompt_embeds=prompt_embeds, negative_prompt_embeds=negative_prompt_embeds, generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed(seed), output= "images" , )[ 0 ] image.save( f" {seed} .png" ) Add a step inside the loop The denoising figure above came from one extra block that records the model's guess of the clean image at every step: from diffusers.modular_pipelines import Flux3AutoBlocks, InputParam, ModularPipelineBlocks, OutputParam class Flux3PreviewStep ( ModularPipelineBlocks ): model_name = "flux3" @property def inputs ( self ): return [InputParam( "latents" ), InputParam( "noise_pred" )] @property def intermediate_outputs ( self ): return [OutputParam( "x0_previews" , type_hint= list )] @torch.no_grad() def __call__ ( self, components, block_state, i, t ): if i == 0 : block_state.x0_previews = [] sigma = t / 1000 # timesteps are sigmas scaled to [0, 1000] block_state.x0_previews.append(block_state.latents - sigma * block_state.noise_pred) # x0 = x_t - sigma * v return components, block_state blocks = Flux3AutoBlocks() denoise_loop = blocks.sub_blocks[ "denoise" ].sub_blocks[ "text2image" ].sub_blocks[ "denoise" ] denoise_loop.sub_blocks.insert( "preview" , Flux3PreviewStep(), 1 ) # between "denoiser" and "after_denoiser" pipe = blocks.init_pipeline(model_id) pipe.load_components(dtype={ "vae" : torch.float32, "default" : torch.bfloat16}) pipe.to( "cuda" ) out = pipe(prompt=prompt, generator=torch.Generator().manual_seed( 0 ), output=[ "x0_previews" , "images" ]) Try it Models: FLUX.3 Image Klein collection Docs: FLUX.3 in Diffusers Fine-tune: DreamBooth LoRA scripts Prompting: Black Forest Labs prompting guide Built something with FLUX.3? items.content: Back to Articles a]:hidden"> Run fast, private agents on-device with LFM2.5-24B-A2B Team Article Published October 13, 2026 Upvote 70 +64 Raahul Vignesh Raahul26 Follow LiquidAI Song Duong sduong Follow LiquidAI Akhilesh Deepak Gotmare akhileshdeepakgotmare Follow LiquidAI Fernando Fernandes Neto fernandofernandes Follow LiquidAI Jiahui Wang WWWjiahui Follow LiquidAI Mayank Agarwal mayankagarwal Follow LiquidAI nathan ranchin nathanrchn Follow LiquidAI Sergei Tilga tilgasergey Follow LiquidAI Sinoué GAD GAD-cell Follow LiquidAI Tim Seyde tseyde Follow LiquidAI Zetian Li zetianli Follow LiquidAI changyi yang changyiyang Follow LiquidAI Simon Lee yungisimon Follow LiquidAI Leonie Monigatti iamleonie Follow LiquidAI Maxime Labonne mlabonne Follow LiquidAI Karthik Macherla karthikrmacherla Follow LiquidAI Alfred Eng alfredeng Follow LiquidAI Khoi Nguyen KTLK Follow LiquidAI Paul Pak paulpak58 Follow LiquidAI xx tugot17 Follow LiquidAI Tarek Dakhran tdakhran Follow LiquidAI Anthony Maltsev amaltsev Follow LiquidAI Aldo Gael Carranza agcarranza Follow LiquidAI Tyler Murray undfined Follow LiquidAI Aditya Tadimeti adityatadimeti Follow LiquidAI Jimmy T.H. Smith jimmysmith1919 Follow LiquidAI Yuri Khrustalev ykhrustalev Follow LiquidAI :last-child]:mb-0"> LFM2.5-24B-A2B is a 24B-parameter reasoning model with just 2B active parameters, built for fast, private agents on-device. It thinks before it answers, calls tools, and works through multi-step tasks inside popular agent harnesses. Because only 2B parameters are active per token, each reasoning token is cheap, so you can run agents continuously on your own hardware. Best-in-class agent: Competitive with Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, a model with ~50% more total and active parameters, on agentic and tool-use tasks, scoring 48.09 on LiveClaw versus 38.19. Reasoning at MoE speed: Always thinks before it answers. With only 2B active parameters per token, each reasoning token is cheap. Efficient inference: 184 tok/s on an Apple M5 Max and up to 21K output tok/s on a single NVIDIA B300 GPU. How we built a reasoning agent with 2B active parameters LFM2.5-24B-A2B builds on LFM2-24B-A2B and keeps its architecture: 40 layers, 64 experts per MoE block with top-4 routing, and the same hybrid of gated short convolutions and GQA. The context window grows from 32K to 131K tokens, and an in-place tokenizer expansion doubles the vocabulary from 65K to 128K tokens for better non-Latin tokenization. Unlike its predecessor, it is a reasoning-only model that produces an explicit chain of thought before its final answer. Pre-training was scaled up from ~17T to ~33T tokens. Mid-training then adds 2T tokens at 32K context, weighted toward reasoning, math, code, instruction following, and multilingual text, and 300B tokens at 131K context, weighted toward long-context data. Tool calls and multi-turn trajectories appear throughout both phases. Post-training turns the base model into an agent in five stages: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) Teacher specialization Multi-domain on-policy distillation (MOPD), non-agentic: distill the specialist teachers on non-agentic tasks. MOPD, agentic: a second distillation stage focused on agentic tasks. Agentic reinforcement learning (Agentic RL): train the model inside agent harnesses, such as OpenClaw , Hermes Agent , Pi , and OpenCode . Benchmark results We evaluated LFM2.5-24B-A2B against Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it, and Nemotron-3.5-Lightning on 16 benchmarks covering tool use and agentic workflows, knowledge, instruction following, math, and coding. It is the smallest model in the group, yet it is competitive with MoEs with ~50% more total and active parameters. Benchmark LFM2.5-24B-A2B Qwen3.6-35B-A3B Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it Nemotron-3.5-Lightning (30B-A3B) AutomationBench 27.69 8.72 5.46 2.61 BFCLv4 65.01 65.00 57.09 53.78 ToolSandbox 80.71 75.02 72.09 75.13 LiveClaw 48.09 38.19 41.25 37.72 PinchBench 83.18 89.93 77.12 84.20 τ³-Bench Banking 8.04 7.63 4.54 7.01 WebArena Verified 26.75 37.62 25.62 28.69 GPQA Diamond 74.42 83.69 74.90 72.42 AA-Omniscience -24.90 -24.35 -59.39 -3.58 HLE 7.40 7.69 8.57 5.65 IFEval 96.75 93.06 92.00 94.19 IFBench 74.69 64.21 47.44 71.67 Multi-IF 84.38 81.53 82.19 82.34 MATH-500 96.04 96.73 95.66 96.40 SWE-Bench Verified (OpenCode) 51.00 66.20 25.80 53.40 SciCode 32.71 37.35 35.42 27.78 *All the models were evaluated with vLLM, using each benchmark's recommended generation parameters. For your app, the strengths are tool use and instruction following. LFM2.5-24B-A2B leads or matches the competition on five of the eight tool-use and agentic benchmarks (AutomationBench, BFCLv4, ToolSandbox, LiveClaw, and τ³-Bench Banking), and on AutomationBench it scores more than three times the next-best model. It also leads on all three instruction-following benchmarks. Larger models keep an edge on knowledge-heavy benchmarks like GPQA Diamond, HLE, and AA-Omniscience, and on coding benchmarks like SWE-Bench Verified (OpenCode) and SciCode, so pair LFM2.5-24B-A2B with retrieval or web search for knowledge-heavy workloads. These results make LFM2.5-24B-A2B a strong foundation for agents that need to reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device. Inference speed on CPU and GPU LFM2.5-24B-A2B ships with day-one support across the inference ecosystem, including llama.cpp, MLX, vLLM, SGLang, and ONNX. Edge inference. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest of the compared MoEs, decoding 184 tokens/s on an M5 Max and 114 tokens/s on a Ryzen AI Max+ 395. That is up to 1.7x faster than the next-best model, while using the least memory. GPU inference. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest model in its size class, reaching over 21K output tokens per second at high concurrency on a single B300. How to use LFM2.5-24B-A2B Reach for LFM2.5-24B-A2B when you need agents that reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device. Install the latest version of transformers (compatible with transformers>=5.0.0 ): pip install -U transformers Then load and run the model: from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer, TextStreamer model_id = "LiquidAI/LFM2.5-24B-A2B" model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained( model_id, device_map= "auto" , dtype= "bfloat16" , # attn_implementation="flash_attention_2" <- uncomment on compatible GPU ) tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id) streamer = TextStreamer(tokenizer, skip_prompt= True , skip_special_tokens= True ) prompt = "What is C. elegans?" input_ids = tokenizer.apply_chat_template( [{ "role" : "user" , "content" : prompt}], add_generation_prompt= True , return_tensors= "pt" , tokenize= True , )[ "input_ids" ].to(model.device) output = model.generate( input_ids, do_sample= True , temperature= 0.1 , top_k= 50 , repetition_penalty= 1.05 , max_new_tokens= 512 , streamer=streamer, ) Use it in your agent harness Serve LFM2.5-24B-A2B locally behind any OpenAI-compatible backend, then point your agent harness at it. For example, with Hermes Agent: hermes config set model.provider custom hermes config set model.base_url http://localhost:8080/v1 hermes config set model.default LFM2.5-24B-A2B hermes config set model.context_length 131072 hermes config set model.api_mode chat_completions hermes config set agent.tool_use_enforcement true The port depends on your serving backend: llama.cpp and MLX use 8080 , vLLM uses 8000 , SGLang uses 30000 , and LM Studio uses 1234 . See the model card for OpenClaw and Pi configs, and our guide for the full setup. Check out our release blog for video examples. Get Started with LFM2.5-24B-A2B Both LFM2.5-24B-A2B and LFM2.5-24B-A2B-Base are open-weight and available on Hugging Face today: Download: LFM2.5-24B-A2B-Base and LFM2.5-24B-A2B on Hugging Face. Use in your harness: follow our guide on how to run a local agent, like OpenClaw, Hermes Agent, and Pi. Fine-tune: adapt LFM2.5-24B-A2B to your task with our fine-tuning tutorials . We can't wait to see what you build. items.fingerprint: open and emergent problems in agentic privacy and security a contextual angle|research.google/blog/open-and-emergent-problems-in-agentic-privacy-and-security-a-contextual-angle
items.title: Open and Emergent Problems in Agentic Privacy and Security: A Contextual Angle
items.description: Generative AI
items.content: Open and Emergent Problems in Agentic Privacy and Security: A Contextual Angle October 5, 2026 Eugene Bagdasarian, Research Scientist, and Marco Gruteser, Principal Scientist, Google Research To be useful, AI agents must understand and be constrained by contextual behavioral norms to ensure they act appropriately. Inspired by the theory of Contextual Integrity, our new workshop report outlines key open research directions across system, model, and user levels to build AI agents users can trust. Quick links Technical report Share We're rapidly transitioning to a computing landscape defined by highly general, increasingly autonomous agents . Driven by large language models (LLMs) that can dynamically generate plans and invoke external tools, these systems offer the potential for AI to seamlessly handle complex, multi-step tasks on our behalf. However, realizing this potential requires solving a key challenge: enabling agent capability while ensuring that agents act appropriately. Today, we share a comprehensive new workshop report, " Open and Emergent Problems in Agentic Privacy and Security: A Contextual Angle ," the result of a collaborative effort bringing together more than 50 academic and industry leaders from numerous institutions. We met at the Google Contextual Agent Privacy and Security (CAPS) Workshop, held in late 2025 in New York City. In this report, you’ll find a breakdown of foundational privacy and security challenges that autonomous agents face today, needing coordinated defenses at the system, model, user, and ecosystem levels. Agentic trade-offs The core challenge of agentic AI is that, for an agent to be useful, it may need to have access to personal data and the ability to take consequential actions across a broad range of contexts. However, this access together with agents’ behavioral flexibility requires meaningfully different approaches from those used in traditional software. Unlike traditional deterministic software, agents differ in three critical dimensions that lead to challenges the research community must address together: Unstructured interfaces and input ambiguity : Agents process instructions in formats like natural language and images, which makes it difficult to define "expected behavior" or protect against adversarial manipulations like prompt injection . Probabilistic control flows : Generative planning leads to probabilistic execution paths that traditional testing methodologies can’t easily secure. Autonomy and delegation : As agents handle longer tasks and delegate sub-tasks to other agents, traditional user oversight becomes less effective and likely insufficient, risking "confirmation fatigue". Agentic AI privacy and security challenges. The contextual lens Given that useful agents may need to share data and complete tasks, we believe that the future of trustworthy agents depends on their ability to reason about, understand, and be constrained by the social norms and appropriateness of their actions— for the specific context in which they operate. But how do we teach an agent to understand "context" and appropriateness? Our report is grounded in the theory of Contextual Integrity (CI), which defines privacy not just as secrecy or control, but as "appropriate information flow" according to established and justifiable social norms. A context-specific informational norm is defined by its actors (who is sending and receiving information about whom), the types of information (specific categories of information, like medical or financial records), and transmission principles (the rules governing the flow, like confidentiality or reciprocity). For example, you might be willing to share your gift shopping list with a virtual shopping assistant, but not your family and friends. Our report extends and generalizes contextual integrity for information sharing to contextual security, that is the appropriateness of agent actions. By anchoring agent privacy and security in CI, we explore how we can design systems that evaluate whether an action is socially and contextually appropriate before executing it. Model of a general AI agent interacting with other users, tools, and agents across contexts. Operationalizing Contextual Integrity For the first time since the development of the theory of Contextual Integrity, LLMs provide an opportunity to create machine readable policy that is truly context dependent. There has historically been a semantic gap between high-level contextual norms and low-level system permissions. For example, “protect my data while organizing my travel for a conference” requires specific instructions on what user information is appropriate to share when booking flights, applying for visas, and communicating with organizers. Traditional methods like manual permissions or expert-written policies cannot scale to a future with AI agents autonomously performing multiple complex, long-running tasks. As language models begin to understand CI , we argue that this gap can be bridged. Our report advocates for complementing model and user interaction advances with a contextual policy engine that forms part of a supervisor layer to monitor and enforce the appropriateness of actions. This policy engine includes a dynamic policy generation loop that can operate in real time (illustrated below) to tailor policies to the user request and open-ended, dynamic contexts, including new tools and capabilities that might be discovered at runtime. This allows the system to evaluate whether a requested data flow is appropriate before any information leaves the user's workspace. An illustrative example of how a contextual policy engine architecture could be instantiated within an agentic system. Multi-layered approach to agentic privacy and security Working towards contextual policy engines together with necessary advances at the model- and user-level results in a multi-layered approach. Our report outlines opportunities for innovation across the entire stack: System-level sandboxing : The execution environment can impose additional guardrails to limit the impact of agent or model failures and facilitate detection and response. Traditional operating systems sandbox applications by statically limiting access, say to files or networks. For agents, we explore dynamically limiting agentic capabilities, establishing agent identity, and authorizing or revoking access to data based on changes in context. Model-level reasoning : An agent performing complex tasks has to judge the appropriateness of its actions, such as sharing user data. Future research should enable models to disambiguate under-specified user prompts and reason about appropriateness under changing contextual norms. User-centric controls : The traditional “Notice and Choice” framework assumes that individuals can make fine-grained decisions about actions affecting personal data and relies on an assumption of foreseeability. However, autonomous agents’ behavior is inherently probabilistic, high volume, and generative. We explore shifting interfaces towards dynamic, contextual, and personalized control mechanisms consistent with user mental models. Multi-agent interactions : So that AI agents can safely collaborate with each other on complex tasks we need to develop effective guardrails to prevent the agents from colluding and violating contextual norms. Ecosystem governance : We explore challenges in governance mechanisms to arrive at a set of contextual norms that are collected and shared across agents. Furthermore, as norms can differ across domains and entities we need mechanisms that allow us to resolve conflicts, negotiate norm changes, and verify compliance. Measuring privacy and security dynamically Finally, we propose the development of new approaches to safety evaluations that more directly apply to highly autonomous, multi-agent systems. Our report highlights the need for standardized, multi-agent benchmarks — dynamic "Agent Gym" environments where researchers can safely simulate complex, cascading interactions during extended periods. With these open-source sandboxes, we can establish a robust, shared privacy, security, and safety baseline across academia and industry. A call to action This is an ambitious project, but a safe, secure, and trustworthy agentic ecosystem is too large a task for any single discipline, organization or sector. Calling for new ideas and unprecedented collaborations, the report lays out foundational opportunities; it is a call to action for the broader research community across academia, government, civil society, and industry to develop the contextual foundations necessary for a safe, secure, and privacy-respecting ecosystem. We invite you to read the technical report . Acknowledgements We would like to thank Lillian Tsai for serving as co-primary author and Sarah de Haas for coordinating the workshop, report writing, and blogpost. Kassem Fawaz, Stefan Mellem, Helen Nissenbaum, and Nina Taft contributed to conceptualization, writing across multiple sections, and guided the writing process. Sebastian Benthall, Madiha Zahrah Choksi, Seliem El-Sayed, Ferdinando Fioretto, Adrià Gascón, Ashish Hooda, Ivan Petrov, Francesco Pinto, Octavian Suciu, Trishita Tiwari, Harold Triedman, Ren Yi, and Wen Zhang served as section leads. We are grateful for the contribution by the over 50 researchers, academic partners, and industry leaders who co-authored the report or participated in workshop discussions. This work was supported by Daniel Ramage, Corinna Cortes, Yossi Matias, Pushmeet Kohli, Hank Levy, Raluca Ada Popa, Amanda Walker, Brendan McMahan, and James Manyika. Eugene Bagdasarian is also an Assistant Professor at University of Massachusetts Amherst. Labels: Generative AI Natural Language Processing Security, Privacy and Abuse Prevention Quick links Technical report Share × ❮ ❯ A system diagram of an AI agent architecture detailing its internal components, behavioral expectations, and its interactions with users and different external contexts. A diagram illustrating three AI security challenges: input ambiguity via prompt injection, non-deterministic control flows, and autonomy and delegation. A flowchart demonstrating a contextual policy architecture where an AI agent's proposed actions are evaluated by a policy engine before being executed by external tools.

items.title: The Agent Said It Was Done. The Database Disagreed.
items.content: Back to Articles a]:hidden"> The Agent Said It Was Done. The Database Disagreed. Enterprise Article Published October 3, 2026 Upvote 90 +84 Tuhin Kundu tuhink Follow microsoft :last-child]:mb-0"> Microsoft ThinkingBox grades AI agents on the records they leave behind, not the sentences they generate, and then asks whether they can do it twenty times in a row. It is now available through Hugging Face. Figure 1: ThinkingBox runs an agent against isolated MCP tool sessions, then grades the terminal backend state and side effects it leaves behind. From our ThinkingBox paper . This is a joint blog by Microsoft and Hugging Face, special thanks to Tommy Guy (founder at Enderis AI, previously Microsoft), Sergio Paniego from Hugging Face and our former interns Zhuochun Li (University of Pittsburgh), Ali Keramati (UC Irvine), Youngmin Ko (Northwestern) for co-authoring/reviewing efforts. A customer writes in. Her $745 kitchen appliance has been stuck in a courier "exception" at a Nashville distribution center, fifteen days past its estimated delivery date. The AI agent does careful work. Nine tool calls: it pulls the order, checks tracking, looks up her customer profile, searches the refund policy twice, confirms no ticket exists, opens one, documents the timeline, and reads the policy correctly; her account segment genuinely does not qualify for late-delivery compensation. Then it closes the ticket as resolved and replies “ Since your query is resolved, is there anything I may assist you with? ” Two things are wrong. The carrier exception is still open, so the required end state was on hold , pending resolution. And the customer never got a real answer to what she actually asked. An AI grader checking tool calls would see nine well-formed ones. The grader checking whether the agent wrote to the database would see that too. The database is what disagrees . That gap is what ThinkingBox measures. Across 507 stateful business workflows, each run 20 times against various LLM models, it grades agents on terminal backend state and side effects. This post covers what we found, what consistency costs, and how to run the benchmark yourself through OpenEnv . You can run this one yourself: the example above is adapted from a benchmark task sandbox_external_retail_group1.py:test_case_ST003_006 , and the executable check that fails is a single field: the ticket's status is solved where the required end state is hold. The full trace is in Appendix D.4, Case 3 of our paper . Contents A tool call is not an outcome One success is not reliability Can you depend on the model behind your agent? What consistency costs Failure signatures How it works Run it yourself Where this goes next Want to try it before reading the results? Skip to section Run it yourself . A tool call is not an outcome Final responses and valid tool calls are only proxies. An agent can sound correct while leaving the wrong value, changing the wrong record, or creating an extra side effect. Only the records it leaves behind settle the question. The gap is substantial. In a common-set ablation covering 121,680 valid trials across 12 LLM models, 79,853 attempts failed the executable checks. Of those failures, 67.24% still terminated cleanly, invoked a state-changing tool, and reported no final tool error. Executable checks nevertheless found wrong field values in 77.61% of them, unintended extra effects in 43.30%, and missing required effects in 25.36%. Those state-check findings overlap. A trajectory is a claim. Database state is the evidence. Repetition is the trust test. One success is not reliability An agent that processes a refund correctly once and mishandles it the next four times is not a working refund agent. So every task runs 20 independent times , each from an identical clean backend, and we report three different things: Table 1: The three numbers we report, and the question each one answers. Metric What it measures What it answers pass@1 Share of all attempts that succeeded How does it usually do? pass@20 Share of tasks solved at least once in 20 tries Can it ever do this? Breadth. Observed 20/20 Tasks that actually passed all 20 recorded attempts Can it always be correct? We use observed 20/20 in this blog post as the literal count of how many of the 507 tasks passed 20 out of 20. No estimator, no smoothing. Starting with the familiar view. The table below reports pass@1, the single-attempt score estimate, broken out by domain. This is the number most leaderboards publish, and on its own it reads like an ordinary capability ranking. Table 2: ThinkingBox-Bench pass@1 (%) by domain. Each model is evaluated on every task for 20 repeated trials. Bold marks the group leader; underline marks the runner-up. The standard errors for the single attempt score estimates are provided in Table 4 in our ThinkingBox paper . Model Retail (98) Auto insurance (100) Travel (104) Neobank (104) Consulting (101) Overall, task-weighted (507) Proprietary models Claude Opus 5.5 80.97 68.40 54.28 71.25 61.58 67.16 Claude Opus 5 80.71 65.80 49.95 70.62 66.19 66.50 GPT-5.4 76.33 62.65 68.12 65.34 54.60 65.36 GPT-5.6 Sol 67.65 65.30 60.34 59.09 57.52 61.91 Claude Sonnet 4.6 72.35 54.40 58.94 56.39 54.31 59.19 GPT-6 Astra 71.73 46.55 55.87 60.87 56.83 58.31 GPT-5.2 70.20 22.40 53.70 51.15 34.06 46.28 Claude Opus 4.6 68.62 8.30 21.11 35.67 27.82 32.09 o3-pro 37.70 2.95 17.31 24.28 14.60 19.31 Grok-4.3 43.93 2.60 15.14 1.78 9.55 14.38 Open-weight models Kimi-K3 82.24 50.80 61.83 41.35 51.63 57.37 Qwen3.8-27B 64.03 47.85 53.41 47.88 45.69 51.70 DeepSeek-V4-Pro 68.21 29.65 43.13 44.86 31.04 43.26 Kimi-K2.6 53.72 24.50 39.52 33.65 37.33 37.66 GLM-5.1 58.67 25.70 35.43 13.27 34.06 33.19 Qwen3.6-27B 43.11 29.00 46.39 27.84 18.37 32.94 Qwen3.5-9B 19.90 0.70 4.71 1.15 2.33 5.65 Mistral-Large-3 11.28 1.30 8.99 1.15 0.74 4.66 Claude Opus 5.5 leads overall at 67.16%, two-thirds of a point above Claude Opus 5. Kimi-K3 is the strongest open-weights model , within a point of GPT-6-Astra. Domain matters just as much : Claude Opus 4.6 scores 68.62% on retail but 8.30% on auto insurance. One good run tells you a model can do the work. It does not tell you whether it will do it again. So run every task 20 times and ask how much of that score survives. Figure 2: How much of each model's single-attempt score survives 20 repeats. Only three hold on to most of their pass@1 scores: GPT-6 Astra retains 78% of its single-attempt rate, and Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Opus 5 each retain 71%. At the other end, GLM-5.1, Kimi-K2.6 and DeepSeek-V4-Pro each keep about 8%. The gap between what a model can do once and what it does every time is the whole story. Can you depend on the model behind your agent? Figure 3: Breadth and consistency pull apart. Twelve of the eighteen models are shown; six below 33% pass@1 are omitted for legibility. Kimi-K3 has the broadest coverage of any model we tested. It solves 93.89% of the benchmark at least once: 476 of 507 tasks. Only 31 tasks defeat it entirely, the lowest count in the field. On retail workflows it leads outright at 82.24% pass@1, ahead of every proprietary model. Kimi-K3 is also among the least consistent. Just 68 of 507 tasks, 13.41%, succeed in all 20 attempts. Claude Opus 5 inverts this. It solves fewer tasks at least once (79.09%; 106 defeat it entirely) but completes 47.53% of the benchmark on every single attempt. A newer model does not fix this. Claude Opus 5.5 scores higher than Claude Opus 5 on every-attempt average, 67.16% against 66.50%, and solves more tasks at least once. It passes exactly the same number of tasks on all 20 attempts: 241. Half a point of headline accuracy bought no additional dependability at all. Kimi-K3 solves 75 more tasks at least once than Opus 5. Opus 5 solves 173 more tasks consistently than Kimi-K3. If you are choosing a model for work that touches real records, pass@20 is the wrong column to look at. What consistency costs Capability comparisons usually stop at the score. For anyone deploying, the relevant question is what a successful unit of work costs. We measure that as cost per successful task attempt. We say task attempt because every benchmark task is run repeatedly and cost is incurred per attempt, so pass@1 is the matching quality denominator. We took each model's recorded token usage from its full 507 × 20 campaign and priced it at undiscounted list rates available on OpenRouter + , reversing promotional discounts and excluding endpoints that declare quantization. Input, output and cache rates all come from one provider endpoint per model. Then we divided one run's cost by the number of attempts that succeeded : Cost per successful task attempt = estimated cost for 507 attempts, one per task ÷ (507 × pass@1) This is a comparative efficiency index, not an invoice, and not the price of serving one production request. It also prices single successes, not consistency. We price consistency next. Example: GPT-5.4 costs $43.49 for 507 attempts (one attempt per task) and has 65.36% pass@1, so $43.49 ÷ (507 × 0.6536) = $0.131 per successful task attempt. Pareto cost frontier A model is on the frontier if no other model is both no more expensive and at least as accurate . Three models qualify; every other model is dominated on at least one axis. Figure 4: Cost per successful task attempt against pass@1. Ringed dots are pareto cost frontier models. The frontier has three steps. GPT-5.6 Sol has the lowest cost per success at $0.127; GPT-5.4 raises pass@1 by 3.45 percentage points for $0.004 more per success; Claude Opus 5.5 adds another 1.80 points at $0.276 per success. Each of the three remains on the cost frontier line because no cheaper model matches its pass@1. Claude Opus 5 is the clearest case: at $0.475 per successful attempt and 66.50% pass@1, it is both more expensive and less accurate than Claude Opus 5.5 at $0.276 and 67.16%. Now price consistency Cost per success rewards a model that is cheap and often right. It does not reward a model that is right every time. So we also compute cost per dependable task: the cost of the full 20-run campaign divided by the number of tasks the model passed on all 20 attempts. Cost per dependable task = estimated cost of 20 runs of 507 attempts ÷ tasks passing 20/20 Example: GPT-6-Astra costs 20 × $86.03 = $1,720.60 for the campaign and passes 231 tasks on every attempt, so $1,720.60 ÷ 231 = $7.45 per dependable task. Table 3: The nine lowest costs per dependable task among models with at least one observed 20/20 task, sorted low to high. Estimated $, not actual cloud bills. Model Tasks passing 20/20 Est. cost, 20 runs Cost per dependable task GPT-5.4 128 (25.25%) $869.80 $6.80 GPT-6 Astra 231 (45.56%) $1,720.60 $7.45 Claude Opus 5.5 241 (47.53%) $1,880.77 $7.80 GPT-5.6 Sol 82 (16.17%) $800.00 $9.76 Claude Opus 5 241 (47.53%) $3,206.00 $13.30 Claude Sonnet 4.6 102 (20.12%) $1,587.60 $15.56 GPT-5.2 44 (8.68%) $878.00 $19.95 Kimi-K3 68 (13.41%) $1,406.40 $20.68 Qwen3.8-27B 38 (7.50%) $925.80 $24.36 Now rank by consistency. GPT-5.4 is the cheapest at $6.80, though only 128 tasks meet the bar. GPT-6 Astra reaches 231 at $7.45, and Claude Opus 5.5 the joint-highest 241 at $7.80. None of the three dominates the others: each additional dependable task costs more. Claude Opus 5 also passes 241, but at $13.30, so Opus 5.5 dominates it outright. GPT-5.6 Sol, the cheapest per single success at $0.127, costs $9.76 per dependable task. The cheapest way to get a right answer is not the cheapest way to get a dependable one. Failure signatures We assign each failed trace one deterministic diagnostic signature, and the headline is actionable: roughly four in five failures are tool handling, not reasoning. Across an ablation study in Table 5 of our paper : Failure signature Share of failures Tool usage 79.9% Wrong state updates 10.3% Incomplete user resolutions 7.0% No state-changing action 2.9% These are unweighted averages of per-model shares and observable labels, not unique causal explanations. The practical pattern is simple: agents usually get far enough to attempt the workflow, then fail to recover from tool errors, failed preconditions, or empty lookups. That is a retry and error-recovery problem before it is a model problem. Difficulty also changes by domain: across the models listed in Table 2 above, retail averages 59.52% pass@1 while auto insurance averages 33.83%. What to do about it. Treat the 20/20 rate as a design input, not a verdict. The same signal the benchmark grades on is available in production: check the terminal state before you commit, not the model's summary of it. Classify tool and system errors so retries target the recoverable ones. Cut the tool surface to what the workflow needs. And require human approval on the changes you cannot cheaply reverse. We have not measured the lift from any of these on this benchmark, which is exactly the kind of thing the environment now makes testable. How it works ThinkingBox is the agent sandbox, while ThinkingBox-Bench is a dataset benchmark to evaluate agents. The diagram at the top of this post shows the loop; here is what each part does. Figure 5: The sandbox loop from panel A in Figure 1 above: isolated tool session, terminal database state, side effects, executable judges. Each task defines a starting backend state, a user goal, the available MCP tools, the domain policy, and executable checks over the terminal state. A simulated user holds private context (a booking reference, a preference, or a date of birth) and releases it only when asked. Every attempt gets an isolated MCP session with freshly initialized state. Two attempts of the same task never share a database row or cached tool state, which is what makes 20-trial comparison meaningful. At the end, a side-effect extractor derives what actually changed, and deterministic judges compare it against the required end state, accepting any trajectory that produces the right outcome while rejecting wrong, missing or extra effects. For requirements with no clean database value ("did the agent disclose this is not guaranteed?"), a narrow binary rubric question handles the semantics. 477 of the 507 tasks are graded on state alone; 30 add response rubrics. The trust boundary: the model sees tasks, dialogue and tool schemas. Golden state, assertions, grading internals and credentials stay on the evaluator side. Run it yourself ThinkingBox is now on Hugging Face, both the harness and the dataset . ThinkingBox-Bench now sits behind the OpenEnv interface, and each finished episode returns a binary pass/fail reward. The released adapter is designed for evaluation; separate, non-benchmark scenarios can use the same interface in training workflows. Before you start Tested on Linux and WSL, with Python 3.11+, uv and Docker. You also need a thinkingbox-data checkout at the pinned release and model endpoints for the agent, simulated user and judge. One endpoint can serve all three roles, which is the simplest way to start. The OpenEnv image starts only the OpenEnv API ; everything else you run yourself. Install # 1. OpenEnv + the ThinkingBox environment git clone https://github.com/huggingface/OpenEnv cd OpenEnv uv sync --project envs/thinkingbox_env --frozen # 2. The executable benchmark, at the pinned release git clone https://github.com/microsoft/thinkingbox-data git -C thinkingbox-data checkout thinkingbox-bench-v1.0 # 3. The ThinkingBox CLI, which provides `tb` uv tool install "thinkingbox @ git+https://github.com/microsoft/thinkingbox" Start Typesense In a second terminal , start Typesense 30.1 and wait for its health check: mkdir -p .typesense-data docker run -- rm -d --name thinkingbox-typesense \ -p 8108:8108 \ -v " $PWD /.typesense-data:/data" \ typesense/typesense:30.1 \ --data-dir /data --api-key=Fake --enable-cors until curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:8108/health; do sleep 1; done Start the MCP servers In a third terminal , start the Session Proxy and MCP servers. cd OpenEnv tb mcp-start --host 127.0.0.1 --port 7111 \ --servers " $PWD /thinkingbox-data/servers/servers.yaml" curl -fsS http://127.0.0.1:7111/health Start the OpenEnv server Back in the first terminal, start the OpenEnv server against a ThinkingBox YAML config naming your three models ( config guide ): OPENENV_TB_CONFIG= " $PWD /thinkingbox.yaml" \ uv run --project envs/thinkingbox_env --frozen server Check readiness Gate on readiness before running anything. It returns 503 until its observable data, configuration and Session Proxy checks pass. It cannot observe Typesense or live-probe every model endpoint, so confirm those separately: curl -sS http://127.0.0.1:8000/ready Score an episode Now score a real episode. example_usage.py only resets and lists tools; for agent actions, effects and assertions use the packaged evaluator: echo "- sandbox_external_retail_group1.py:test_case_ST002_001" > one_task.yaml uv run --project envs/thinkingbox_env thinkingbox-eval \ one_task.yaml \ --config " $PWD /thinkingbox.yaml" \ --output results.jsonl \ --errors-output errors.jsonl \ --repeat 1 --message-timeout 1800 The OpenEnv adapter writes operational failures to an errors sidecar so they can be rerun rather than silently mixed with model outcomes. A canonical result must resolve or explicitly account for those attempts; we counted system errors as unsuccessful trials. Runs are gated on a pinned framework commit, a pinned data release and a bundle hash, so a canonical result is verifiable rather than asserted. Where this goes next The useful part of this work is not our pass@1 leaderboard. It is the environment. If you are evaluating an agent that touches real records: Inspect a failure. Find a run that terminated cleanly and still failed, and look at what actually changed in the database. It reframes what your own evals measure. Reproduce one task through OpenEnv with your own model. Report a repeat metric, and define it. Whatever k your use case justifies; say whether you are reporting best-of-k or every-of-k, and how you computed it.
